consent.label: Yes — Liivv may keep and use my health answers.

body.1: The answers on this page are health information about you.
body.2: If you tick the box, Liivv keeps them on your health profile and uses them to decide which guidance, chapters and reminders you see in your account, and so our pharmacy team can answer your questions with your situation in front of them.

new-to-the-journey.title: New to the Journey
new-to-the-journey.heroBody: Just been told you need surgery, or just home with a new stoma — calm answers for both, plus the one thing to ask for before you go in.
new-to-the-journey.focus: Before surgery: what to expect, stoma siting, questions to ask, and supporting someone. After surgery: first weeks, change routines, starter supplies, who to ask, and soft next steps.
new-to-the-journey.vibe: Supportive and demystifying — a soft place to land.

categoriesIntro.heading: You are not supposed to know everything yet
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter covers both sides of the operation. If surgery is still ahead of you, start at the top. If you are already home, skip to First Week Basics — nothing above it will be news.

1.title: You have just been told you need one

items.1: Feeling frightened, angry, or numb is an ordinary reaction to this news, not a sign you are handling it badly
items.2: The waiting is hard, and recovery has its own hard parts. Hospitals aim to teach you the pouch change before you go home, and it gets easier with practice; adjusting takes time
items.3: People with ostomies work, travel, swim, date, have children, and play sport. That is the ordinary outcome, not the exceptional one — most of it comes back as you recover. How long that takes varies, and your surgeon sets the pace for lifting, work and exercise

1.note: It does get easier. If it is not easing, or you are struggling to get through the day, tell your NSWOC or doctor rather than waiting it out — low mood after this surgery is common and treatable. If you want to talk to someone who has been through it, Ostomy Canada trains peer visitors: ask your surgeon or NSWOC for a referral, or contact your local chapter yourself. See Everyday Liivving.

1.prompt: If it is not easing, or you are struggling to get through the day

2.prompt: If you want to talk to someone who has been through it
2.detail: Ask your surgeon or NSWOC for a referral, or contact your local chapter yourself.

2.title: Ask for stoma siting — this one matters most

items.1: Siting means an NSWOC or your surgeon marks the best spot on your abdomen before your operation, while you are awake. Your surgeon makes the final call during surgery, so sometimes more than one spot is marked
items.2: They check the spot while you sit, stand, and bend, and keep it clear of your waistband, skin folds, scars, and your beltline
items.3: Placement affects how well every appliance you ever wear will seal, and people marked before surgery tend to have fewer leaks. If leaks do happen they are usually fixable with a different appliance or an added seal, whatever the shape of your abdomen

2.note: This is the thing people most often do not know to ask for, and it is much harder to fix afterwards. If nobody has mentioned siting, ask. That includes emergency surgery — Canadian guidance says emergency patients should still be marked before the anesthetic wherever possible, and it matters more then, not less.

3.title: Questions worth asking before you go in

items.1: Which type of ostomy, and is it expected to be permanent or reversible? If reversible, roughly when might that be considered?
items.2: Will I be seen by an NSWOC before surgery for siting, and who will teach me afterwards?
items.3: What will my output be like, and what should I expect in the first weeks?

categoriesIntro.heading: Know your setup
categoriesIntro.body: A pouching system is a skin barrier (wafer/flange) plus a pouch. Fit and skin health drive comfort more than anything else.

items.1: Colostomy, ileostomy, and urostomy each shape output and daily care a little differently
items.2: A stoma can be temporary or permanent — your care team decides with you
items.3: Healthy peristomal skin should look like the skin on the other side of your abdomen

2.title: The less common diversions

1.heading: Other stomas you may hear about

items.1: Jejunostomy — formed higher in the small bowel than an ileostomy. Output is greater and more watery, and fluid, salt and nutrition need closer specialist follow-up
items.2: Ileal conduit — the most common form of urostomy, where urine is diverted through a short piece of bowel to a stoma
items.3: Nephrostomy — a tube that drains urine straight from the kidney. It comes out through the skin of your back rather than through a stoma on the abdomen, and drains into a bag usually strapped to your thigh under your clothes. It is often temporary

2.heading: Continent diversions, which work differently

items.1: An ileoanal pouch (often called a J-pouch) is designed to leave you with no stoma in the long run — an internal reservoir is joined to the anus, so you pass stool the usual way. It normally takes two or three operations, and most people have a temporary ileostomy for a few months in between. Once it is working, stool is looser and you go more often, commonly five to ten times a day, settling with time
items.2: A continent ileostomy, such as a Kock pouch, has a small flush stoma and an internal reservoir made from small bowel. There is no pouch to wear — you drain it with a catheter, usually two to four times a day, and cover the stoma with a cap or gauze in between
items.3: A Mitrofanoff is a different operation, for urine rather than stool. A narrow channel, usually made from the appendix, runs from your own bladder to a small stoma, and you pass a catheter through it to empty

2.note: Continent diversions are cared for quite differently from a conventional stoma. Advice about pouches, barriers and flanges will not apply to you — advice about diet, fluids and salt still does. Two things this site does not cover. With a bowel reservoir such as a Kock pouch, if the catheter will not pass, stop rather than persisting, rest an hour and try again, and get advice that day if you still cannot drain. With a Mitrofanoff, which drains urine, do not keep trying — an unemptied bladder needs an emergency department the same day. Your surgical team and NSWOC are the right source for both.
NSWOCC publishes free patient guides for several of these, including jejunostomy and gastrostomy, in English and French. They are linked from Everyday Liivving.

items.1: Appliance or pouching system — the whole setup: the barrier plus the pouch
items.2: Barrier, wafer or baseplate — the part that sticks to your skin. Many people say flange for this too, but on some two-piece systems flange means the plastic ring that clicks the pouch on. If you are ordering, check which one your brand means
items.3: Convexity — a barrier that curves outward towards your skin instead of lying flat, to help a flat or retracted stoma stand out or to smooth a crease. It comes in soft and firm versions and different depths. Helpful for some abdomens, harmful for others, so it is an assessment rather than a purchase

items.1: Peristomal skin — the skin around the stoma. It starts where the stoma meets your skin and takes in everything your barrier, tape or belt touches
items.2: Output — what comes out of the stoma. You will hear it used far more often than you might expect
items.3: Mucocutaneous junction — where the stoma meets your skin

items.1: NSWOC — Nurse Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence. The Canadian specialist for stoma care, and the term used nationally
items.2: ET nurse or enterostomal therapy nurse — the older term for the same role. It still appears in official documents, including Saskatchewan’s SAIL program rules
items.3: WOCN Society — the American organization, which you will meet in US-published material. There the nurse is a WOC nurse, and a certified one is a CWOCN

1.def: The whole setup: the barrier plus the pouch.

2.def: The part that sticks to your skin. Guides also call it a flange.

3.def: Where output collects. A drainable pouch is emptied and closed again, a closed pouch is thrown away after use, and a urostomy pouch has a tap for draining urine.

4.def: On a two-piece, the pouch attaches to the barrier. On a one-piece, the barrier and pouch are joined permanently.

items.1: One-piece: barrier and pouch are joined — simple and low-profile
items.2: Two-piece: barrier stays while you change pouches — flexible for frequent emptying
items.3: Your NSWOC or pharmacist can help you find what seals best for your body

items.1: Clean with warm water; avoid oils, fragrances, and lotion under the barrier
items.2: Pat dry completely — dry skin seals better than damp skin
items.3: Powder, paste, rings, and wipes are tools for seal and comfort. Add only what you need, and ask your NSWOC which ones fit your skin.

items.1: Empty drainable pouches at about one-third to one-half full
items.2: Closed pouches are replaced as needed through the day
items.3: Full system changes are often every few days — or sooner if you feel burning, itching, or a leak

9.title: Measure before you order

items.1: Use the measuring guide that comes in the box — hold it over the stoma and pick the closest shape and size
items.2: Cut so the opening sits close to the edge of the stoma. Too large exposes skin to output; too small can rub or injure the stoma
items.3: Not all stomas are round. Many are oval, and a cut-to-fit barrier can be shaped to match

9.note: Re-measure at every change for the first six to eight weeks after surgery, and again after any weight change or a hernia. A barrier cut to a size from before your last weight change is one of the most common reasons a system that used to work suddenly does not.

1.heading: What tends to suit a one-piece

items.1: You want the lowest profile under clothes, and the simplest routine
items.2: Your skin is settled and you are not changing the pouch more often than the barrier

2.heading: What tends to suit a two-piece

items.1: You empty or swap pouches often and would rather not disturb the barrier each time
items.2: You want to alternate between a closed pouch for going out and a drainable one at home
items.3: Reaching or dexterity is difficult, and doing the two steps separately is easier

2.note: Neither is better. Plenty of people use both — a two-piece for workdays and a one-piece for swimming, for instance.

11.title: Flat or convex — please ask before you switch

items.1: A flat barrier suits a stoma that protrudes onto reasonably even skin, which is most people
items.2: Convexity curves toward your skin to help a flat or retracted stoma stand out, or to smooth a dip or crease that output keeps tracking into
items.3: It comes in soft and firm versions and different depths, and the right one depends on your abdomen, your stoma, and how your skin behaves under pressure

11.note: This is the one product decision on the whole site that we would rather you did not make alone. Convexity applied to the wrong abdomen can cause a pressure injury, and it is a common reason people end up with skin damage they did not have before. Ask your NSWOC to assess you — most will let you try one before you buy a box.

items.1: Barrier rings and seals — mouldable, they fill small dips and add a little protection right at the stoma edge
items.2: Paste — not glue. It is a filler for creases and uneven skin. Most contain alcohol, so it can sting on broken skin
items.3: Stoma powder — for weepy, broken skin only, dusted on and the excess brushed off. It does not belong under an intact barrier on healthy skin
items.4: Barrier film or wipes — a thin protective layer between adhesive and skin, useful if removal is irritating your skin

2.heading: For comfort and confidence

items.1: Adhesive remover — reduces the pulling on your skin at removal, which matters more the more often you change
items.2: Belts — add security and are sometimes recommended alongside convexity. They need sizing
items.3: Lubricating deodorant — helps output drop to the bottom of the pouch and controls odour, which also helps with pancaking

2.note: What none of them do is rescue a barrier that is the wrong size or the wrong shape for you. If you are reaching for two or three accessories to make one system stay on, the system is the problem — that is a fit review, not a shopping list.

13.title: Try it before you buy a box

items.1: Hollister, Coloplast and Convatec all send free samples in Canada, whether or not you buy from them, and regardless of which brand you currently use
items.2: Ask for a sample of anything you are considering switching to — barriers, rings, convex products, belts
items.3: Give a new product a few changes before deciding. First impressions are often about unfamiliarity rather than fit

13.note: Their contact details are in Everyday Liivving. There is no obligation attached, and it is a much cheaper way to find what works than buying full boxes.

14.title: When to ask for a fit review

items.1: Leaks that have started happening when they were not before
items.2: Weight change in either direction, which alters the shape of the area around your stoma
items.3: A new bulge, or the skin around the stoma changing shape
items.4: Skin that is not fully healed by the next change
items.5: Pregnancy, or any further abdominal surgery

14.note: A fit review is a normal part of ostomy care, not an admission that something has gone wrong. Bodies change, and the system that suited you last year may simply not be the right one now.

items.1: Re-measure. Stoma size changes over the first six to eight weeks after surgery, and again after a weight change — an opening cut to last month’s size is one of the most common causes of a leak
items.2: Check where the leak starts — from under the barrier, or from the edge. They point at different problems
items.3: Make sure skin is completely dry before the barrier goes on, and hold it in place so body heat can set the seal

2.heading: When to call your NSWOC
2.note: Repeated leaking usually means the fit is wrong, not that you are doing it wrong. Convexity, rings and pastes can all help — but which one depends on your abdomen and your stoma, so that is an assessment rather than a shopping decision. The wrong convexity can cause a pressure injury.

items.1: Leaks more than occasionally, or a pattern you cannot explain
items.2: Skin that has not fully healed between changes

items.1: The pouch film sticks to itself, so output cannot drop away from the stoma and pushes up under the barrier instead
items.2: It is more common with thicker output and with filters that pull the air out quickly

2.heading: What often helps
2.note: If it is constant, or your output has become noticeably thicker than it used to be, mention it — that is worth looking at rather than working around.

items.1: A puff of air in the pouch before you close it
items.2: A lubricating deodorant, which helps output slide to the bottom

items.1: Filters do wet out and stop working — that is normal rather than a fault
items.2: Gas patterns often settle over the first months as your gut adjusts
items.3: Eating and drinking more slowly means swallowing less air

2.heading: When to call your NSWOC
2.note: Food affects gas differently for everyone, and post-surgery advice differs by ostomy type — so this is a conversation with your team or a dietitian rather than a list to follow.

items.1: A sudden change in gas alongside pain, or output that stops

1.heading: Please do not self-diagnose this one

items.1: Irritation from output, a fungal rash, a contact allergy, and a few less common conditions look almost identical to the eye
items.2: They have opposite treatments — the wrong one makes several of them worse

2.heading: What is safe to do meanwhile
2.note: Any skin that is broken, weeping, bleeding, or still not healed by the next change needs an NSWOC to look at it — not a product recommendation from the internet.

items.1: Keep the area clean with warm water only — no oils, lotions, or fragranced products under the barrier
items.2: Check the opening is not cut larger than the stoma, which leaves skin exposed to output
items.3: Photograph it before your appointment, since skin changes between changes

1.heading: Why it matters more with an ileostomy

items.1: An ileostomy puts out more fluid and more salt, so dehydration builds faster and less obviously than people expect
items.2: Thirst is not a reliable early sign — dark urine, headache, and feeling washed out often come first

2.heading: When to call
2.note: High output is the leading reason people are readmitted after ostomy surgery. It is worth phoning about early rather than waiting to see.

items.1: A sustained jump in output lasting more than a day
items.2: Watery, high-volume output that is not settling
items.3: Feeling dizzy, confused, or unusually weak alongside it

items.1: A parastomal hernia — the abdominal wall weakening around the stoma. It is common and it is not something you caused
items.2: It often changes how your barrier sits, so leaks can start at the same time

2.heading: When to call your NSWOC
2.note: Support garments help many people, but they have to be sized and chosen for the specific hernia — buying one without an assessment can make the fit worse rather than better.

items.1: Any new bulge, or a change in the shape of the area around your stoma
High-waisted styles and soft layers can keep a pouch secure and low-profile
items.2: Support belts or wraps for active days when you want extra hold
items.3: You do not have to hide your pouch — comfort and preference come first

items.1: Empty when the pouch is about one-third to one-half full to reduce leak risk
items.2: Pack supplies in your carry-on — never only in checked bags
items.3: Plan bathroom stops the way you plan coffee: early and without apology

items.1: Talk about what helps you feel secure — timing, clothing, or a support wrap
items.2: Confidence grows with a routine that has already worked at home
items.3: Your pace is the right pace

items.1: Many people prefer morning changes when output is often lower
items.2: Lay out supplies like a station before you start
items.3: Restock before you run low — clockwork beats last-minute stress

25.title: Hernias, lifting and your core

items.1: A parastomal hernia is a bulge beside the stoma, where the abdominal wall has weakened and what is underneath pushes through. It is common, and more likely the longer you have a stoma. Ordinary daily life does not cause it, though not smoking, keeping to a healthy weight and avoiding straining all lower the risk
items.2: Follow the lifting advice your surgical team gives you, and ask them to show you how to lift rather than only what to avoid. Your abdominal wall is still healing in the early weeks, so build up gradually — technique matters more than a fixed weight limit
items.3: Gentle core and breathing exercises usually start within the first few days, and you build from there. What is right for you depends on your fitness as much as your surgery — a physiotherapist can set the pace with you

25.note: Many people find a support garment comfortable and reassuring, particularly if a hernia is already there. It is worth knowing that support wear has not been shown to prevent a hernia — it is for comfort and confidence. If you have one, ask your NSWOC to measure and fit you, since a garment that is too tight can restrict your movement and breathing.

26.title: Getting back to activity

items.1: Walking usually comes first and starts early. Everything beyond that is a conversation about timing with your surgical team
items.2: Swimming is fine once your wounds are fully healed — your pouch is water-resistant and, fitted well, designed not to leak. Change it well before you swim rather than just beforehand so the adhesive can settle, and cover the filter with the sticker provided
items.3: Contact sports are worth raising, since a stoma guard protects against a direct blow. Heavy lifting is a separate question — a guard does not help there. Technique, breathing out on the effort and building up gradually do, and most people get back to what they did before

26.note: Ostomy Canada and the manufacturer support programs both run activity resources, and plenty of ostomates return to running, swimming, weights, and team sport.

urgent.heading: Some things are not a website question
urgent.intro: Most stoma worries can wait for your next NSWOC appointment. These cannot. Seek urgent medical care if you notice:
urgent.action: Go to your nearest emergency department or call 911. Do not wait for a callback, and do not troubleshoot a dusky stoma at home.

signs.1: A stoma that turns dark, dusky, purple, or feels cold to the touch
signs.2: Severe abdominal pain, or vomiting with no output for several hours — this can mean a blockage
signs.3: Heavy or continuous bleeding from the stoma itself, not just a spot from cleaning
signs.4: Fever, or skin around the stoma that is hot, spreading red, and painful
signs.5: Confusion, severe dizziness, or very dark urine alongside high output — signs of significant dehydration
signs.6: A Mitrofanoff you cannot pass a catheter through — an unemptied bladder will not wait. A bowel reservoir such as a Kock pouch is different: see “The less common diversions” in Chapter 02 for what to try first

pharmacist.heading: Ask without the awkward
pharmacist.body: Not sure if you need convex, a ring, or a different wipe? Chat with an Ontario pharmacist during business hours — until 5 p.m. Eastern. For clinical stoma concerns, your NSWOC remains your primary resource.

closing.heading: Comfort is a skill you build
closing.body: Knowing your stoma is not a test — it is a quieter relationship with fit, skin, and the products that earn their place on your shelf.

everyday-liivving.heroBody: Eating again, and everything around the edges of a day — travel, winter, money, and the people and programs that exist in Canada.
everyday-liivving.focus: Adding foods back and what to watch for, fluid and salt, gas and odour, the medication question, and then the practical Canadian ones — flying, winter adhesion, going remote, ordering across provincial lines, what coverage actually looks like province by province, and how to find people near you.

categoriesIntro.eyebrow: You are not doing this alone
categoriesIntro.heading: What exists, and who it is for
categoriesIntro.body: Two halves. The first is your own body settling into a routine — what you eat, what comes out, and what changes. The second is everything around it: the money, the travel, and the help that exists in Canada but is almost never in one place. Most of that half links out, because those organizations do it better than we could.

1.title: Peer support is its own kind of care
1.note: A peer visitor is not a substitute for your NSWOC. Most people find they want both.

items.1: Ostomy Canada Society runs chapters and peer support groups across the country, searchable by distance from where you live
items.2: Their Visitor Program trains people who have an ostomy to talk with people who have just had one — lived experience, not clinical advice
items.3: If you are between roughly 20 and 40, ask about Gutsy Gang social clubs — they run in Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Toronto, and Niagara

2.title: What your surgery actually changed

items.1: Food is broken down in the stomach and small intestine, and that part is usually unchanged — this is why you still absorb your nutrition
items.2: The colon’s main job is reclaiming water and salt from what is left, and forming stool. A colostomy leaves most of that intact; an ileostomy bypasses it almost entirely
items.3: A urostomy does not change how food is digested. It carries urine from the kidneys out through the stoma, so it no longer reaches the bladder, and most of the food questions here are not yours. Fluid is the opposite: you need more of it than before, steadily through the day, because a well-flushed system is what protects against infection and stones. Ask your urologist or NSWOC what daily target fits you

2.note: This is the single most useful thing to understand: an ileostomy is not "a colostomy higher up". The missing colon is why output is looser, why fluid and salt matter more, and why the advice differs.

3.title: The first few weeks

items.1: Most teams suggest a lower-fibre period straight after surgery. It is temporary, and it is about swelling at the stoma rather than about fibre being bad for you
items.2: Your stoma is swollen at first and shrinks over the following weeks, so the opening it can pass comfortably gets bigger too
items.3: Appetite is often poor early on. Small, frequent meals tend to sit better than three large ones

3.note: How long this lasts is your surgical team’s call, not a fixed rule — it varies by surgery and by person. Ask when you should be moving on rather than assuming.

1.body: Softer foods may be easier in about the first 2 to 4 weeks. Fibre is okay after surgery; higher-fibre foods are added slowly.

2.body: Soft, lower-fibre foods for about the first 6 to 8 weeks while the stoma is swollen. Then higher-fibre foods are added gradually, one at a time, and chewed well.

4.title: Adding foods back

items.1: One new food at a time, in a small amount, with a couple of days before the next one — otherwise you cannot tell what caused what
items.2: Chew far more than feels necessary. With an ileostomy especially, chewing is doing work your colon used to do
items.3: Keep a rough note for a few weeks. Patterns show up quickly and then you can stop writing things down

4.note: Tolerance is genuinely individual. Two people with the same surgery often land on completely different lists, so treat anyone else’s "foods to avoid" list — including one you find online — as a starting hypothesis rather than a rule.

5.title: Foods people often find need care

1.heading: Commonly reported as harder to pass

items.1: Fibrous or stringy foods — celery, corn, mushrooms, coconut, pineapple, dried fruit
items.2: Skins, pips and casings — apple peel, sweetcorn, nuts, popcorn, sausage skins

2.heading: How to approach them rather than avoid them forever

items.1: Cut small, cook well, chew thoroughly, and try a small amount on a day when you are not out
items.2: Plenty of people go back to all of these. The point is caution, not a permanent ban

2.note: If you have an ileostomy and have had a blockage before, talk to your NSWOC or a dietitian before reintroducing this group. That is a different conversation from a first attempt.

6.title: Fluid and salt

items.1: With an ileostomy you lose more water and more sodium than you did before, and you lose it steadily rather than noticeably
items.2: Thirst is a late signal. Darker urine, headache, cramps, and feeling flat often arrive first
items.3: Plain water alone can sometimes make high output worse — an oral rehydration solution replaces salt as well as fluid

6.note: Ask your NSWOC or pharmacist what to keep at home before you need it. Rehydration solutions are cheap, keep well, and are far more useful bought in advance than at 2am.

items.1: Gas usually settles over the first months as your gut adapts — early gas is not a sign of how things will stay
items.2: Swallowed air is a bigger contributor than most people expect: eating quickly, straws, chewing gum, fizzy drinks
items.3: Filters wet out and stop working. That is the filter doing its job and reaching the end of it, not a defect

items.1: Starchy foods — white rice, pasta, bread, potato without skin, banana, smooth peanut butter, marshmallows

2.heading: Often reported as loosening

items.1: Very sugary drinks, alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, and large amounts of fruit

2.note: These are patterns many people notice, not instructions. If you are using food to manage persistent high output rather than an occasional day, that needs an NSWOC or dietitian rather than a longer list of foods.

9.title: The medication question

items.1: Extended-release, slow-release and enteric-coated tablets are designed to dissolve over a long stretch of gut — with an ileostomy they can pass straight through, intact and unabsorbed
items.2: People sometimes see whole tablets in the pouch. That is worth reporting rather than ignoring
items.3: This can quietly affect anything that matters — blood pressure, thyroid, mental health medication, contraception

9.note: Bring your full medication list to a pharmacist and say you have an ileostomy. There is often an immediate-release or liquid alternative. Do not stop or change anything yourself.

items.1: Pack your supplies in your carry-on. CATSA permits ostomy supplies in both carry-on and checked baggage, so split them — enough in the carry-on to cover the whole journey and a delay, and a backup set in the checked bag. Never let the only set be the one in the hold
items.2: Take roughly twice what you expect to need for the trip
items.3: Cut your barriers to size before you leave, so they are ready if you need to change on the plane. Scissors are not the reason — in Canada, blades of 6 cm or less are allowed in carry-on. Pre-cutting simply spares you cutting a barrier on a tray table, and scissors rules are tighter in some other countries

2.heading: Security

items.1: CATSA permits ostomy supplies in both carry-on and checked baggage, so you should not be turned back for carrying them — though the final decision on any item rests with the screening officer
items.2: Being medical supplies is not a blanket exemption from the liquids rule. That exemption covers prescription and essential non-prescription medication, and CATSA states that ostomy paste tubes must be 100 mL or less and travel in your clear 1 L bag. Treat adhesive remover, barrier spray and lubricating deodorant the same way, or pack full sizes in checked baggage
items.3: You can ask for privacy. CATSA says you can request a private screening room, and if a physical search or a swab is needed you can ask for that to be done there. It helps to tell the officer you have an ostomy pouch, and roughly where it is, before screening starts
items.4: Ostomy Canada publishes a printable Traveller’s Communication Card, and Coloplast Care offers a travel certificate to people enrolled in its program. Convatec’s card is written for US screening and its travel pass is a UK document, so check which version you are getting. None of these is an official pass and CATSA does not require documentation — the card simply saves explaining

2.note: Screening rules change and vary by country. Check CATSA’s current guidance before you fly, and note that it covers flights leaving Canada — for the return leg, check the rules where you are flying out of. What CATSA allows in your carry-on leaving Toronto is not a guarantee coming back.

items.1: Cabin pressure falls in flight, so gas already in the pouch expands a little. In practice the effect is small and a filtered pouch vents most of it — Ostomy Canada is explicit that the pouch will not blow up
items.2: If your pouch does balloon on a flight, the cause is usually swallowed air, fizzy drinks, gassy food, or sitting still for hours. Vent or empty it and carry on
items.3: Empty before boarding and again during the flight rather than waiting for it to feel necessary. An aisle seat makes that discreet rather than an event

11.title: Winter, and why things stop sticking

items.1: Adhesive works less well when it is cold. A barrier that has been in a cold car or an unheated porch will not bond as readily
items.2: Warm the barrier before applying — hold it between your palms for a minute, or tuck it under your clothing against your body — then press it in place for a full minute or two. Use body heat only: not a hairdryer, radiator or microwave. Too much heat damages the adhesive, and because the stoma has no nerve endings it cannot warn you when something is too hot
items.3: If your wear time drops every winter, start with the temperature of your supplies rather than your skin — a barrier stored or carried cold is the more likely explanation

11.note: Store spare supplies somewhere room temperature — Ostomy Canada suggests roughly 15 to 30°C — rather than a garage, shed, or the trunk of a car. Coloplast’s instructions for use state the product must not be stored under freezing conditions. Heat is a problem too, so those same spots are worth avoiding in July as much as in January.

12.title: Cottage, camping and going remote

items.1: Find out where the nearest pharmacy is and how long it would take to reach — but treat it as a backup, not a plan. Pharmacies carry a limited range and are unlikely to stock your exact barrier and pouch
items.2: Take at least double what you need. There is no version of this trip where running out is a minor inconvenience
items.3: Plan disposal, and keep the contents and the pouch separate in your head. Contents go into a toilet where there is one; in the backcountry treat them as any human waste — a cathole 15 to 20 cm deep, at least 60 m from water, trails and camp, or packed out where that is the rule. The pouch itself never goes down a toilet: it blocks the line, and a septic system or holding tank is far less forgiving than a municipal one

12.note: If you irrigate, think it through carefully before committing to somewhere without running water. A routine needs roughly 500 to 1,000 mL of lukewarm water clean enough to drink, about an hour at a toilet, and somewhere for the output to go — and it repeats every day or two. Cold water causes cramping, which is harder to manage away from a tap. If you would not drink the water, do not irrigate with it.

13.title: Ordering across provincial lines

items.1: Your entitlement is set by the province you live in — you qualify through your provincial coverage, not through the store. That does not mean you can buy anywhere
items.2: Ontario and Quebec pay a set amount and leave the choice of retailer to you. Saskatchewan will reimburse products bought in another province if you send a paid receipt showing what you purchased
items.3: Alberta works differently: AADL requires you to buy from an approved Alberta vendor, does not fund online-only shops, and does not reimburse people who buy on their own. In Manitoba you do not buy at all — supplies are ordered through the provincial program and shipped from Winnipeg. In British Columbia, anything ordered online has to come from a PharmaCare-authorized provider

13.note: Check your own program’s vendor rules before you order from out of province — including from us. Moving provinces is a different situation entirely and resets your coverage; that is in Funding & Coverage.

14.title: Supplies people offer you

items.1: Supply exchanges exist, including Facebook groups such as Ostomy Supplies Exchange Canada, and some people do find what they need this way. Ostomy Canada also advises caution: a barrier that suited someone else’s stoma, or one stored badly, can leak or damage your skin
items.2: Check the expiry date, that packaging is intact and unopened, and that the size matches what you use. Ask how the supplies were stored too — heat and damp shorten the life of an adhesive barrier well before its printed expiry
items.3: Do not accept anything whose inner packaging has been opened. Most pouches and barriers are supplied non-sterile, so the reason is less about sterility than the adhesive: once the seal is broken you cannot tell how long it has been exposed to air

14.note: Local chapters and support groups often take in surplus supplies and pass them to members who need them. Friends of Ostomates Worldwide Canada also collects surplus, but ships it to partner organizations overseas rather than to individuals here — it states it cannot support individual requests. If you are donating, it asks that items stay in their packaging.

15.title: What coverage actually looks like in Canada
15.note: We have checked every province and territory against its own government page — see Funding & Coverage for what yours pays, who has to sign off, and the dates that catch people out.

items.1: There is no national ostomy program. The amount, the model, and who approves it all change at the provincial border
items.2: Moving provinces resets everything — including which forms you file and who has to sign them
items.3: Who signs off changes at the border: a physician or nurse practitioner in Ontario and Nova Scotia, nobody clinical in Quebec or British Columbia, and a registered nurse — usually an NSWOC — in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Saskatchewan will not accept a self-application at all

items.1: All three major manufacturers run free support programs — samples, phone lines, and access to ostomy nurses
items.2: You do not have to buy from us, or from them, to use these
items.3: They will also help you work out what your province covers, which is often the fastest way to get an answer

items.1: World Ostomy Day runs every three years, not every year — the last was 4 October 2025, and the next falls in 2028
items.2: In the years between, Canada still marks the first Saturday of October, anchored by Ostomy Canada’s Step Up for Ostomy campaign
items.3: Chapters usually run local events — the chapter finder is the fastest way to see what is happening near you

18.title: Stories from people who have one

items.1: Reading someone describe their first month is worth more than any checklist we could write
items.2: We are collecting stories from Canadians with ostomies — surgery, work, travel, dating, sport, all of it
items.3: If you would like to share yours, tell the care team and we will be in touch about how it works

programsBand.heading: Four ways provinces pay — knowing yours saves you money

1.heading: A flat grant, paid to you
1.body: Ontario and Quebec send a set amount each year and you buy your own supplies. If you use more than the grant covers, the overage is yours — and may be claimable as a medical expense.

2.heading: A percentage cost-share
2.body: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Newfoundland cover a share and you pay the rest, often up to an annual cap. Low income can reduce your share to nothing.

3.heading: Supplies issued to you
3.body: Manitoba does not reimburse — the program sends the supplies. You are registered through an NSWOC after surgery rather than applying yourself.

4.heading: Only if you qualify
4.body: PEI is income-tiered. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick route by category — seniors, social assistance, or specific programs — so there is no general coverage to apply for.

1.heading: Support that is already out there
1.body: These are run by patient organizations and specialist nurses, not by us. They are free, and they are better at this than any retailer.

1.title: Find a chapter or peer support group
1.body: Search by distance from your postal code, from 10 km out to 500 km. Also lists Gutsy Gang social clubs for younger adults.

2.title: Visitor Program
2.body: Trained peer visitors who have an ostomy themselves. Requested through your local chapter, usually after a referral from your surgeon or NSWOC.

3.title: Find an NSWOC near you
3.body: Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence — the clinical specialists for stoma care in Canada. Many hospitals have one; some see outpatients for life.

4.title: Youth Camp
4.body: A week at Camp Horizon in Bragg Creek, Alberta, for kids and teens with ostomies. Partial and full funding is available — ask, do not assume the fee is the barrier.

2.heading: Manufacturer support, compared plainly
2.body: All three are free and none of them require you to buy from us. We have listed what each program offers — not whose products are better, which is not our call to make. All three are run by companies that sell ostomy supplies. Read how each one uses your information before you enrol.

1.title: Secure Start
1.body: Free personalized support regardless of which brand you use, including help navigating coverage. Canadian line: 1-800-263-7421.

2.title: Coloplast Care
2.body: Ongoing educational support, phone access, samples, and the MyOstomy app for tracking changes and output. Consumer support: 1-866-293-6349.

3.title: me+
3.body: Staged around the journey — before surgery, right after, and living with one. Includes video appointments with a certified ostomy nurse. 1-800-465-6302.

3.heading: Coverage and tax help
3.body: Amounts and rules change, and they change by province. Always confirm against the official source before you plan around a number.

1.title: Provincial government programs
1.body: The best public summary of what each province and territory covers, with links through to the official program pages.

2.title: Disability Tax Credit (form T2201)
2.body: Applied for under the “eliminating” category, but having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own — the funding section walks through the test the CRA actually applies. Approval can unlock the RDSP and other credits, so it is worth reading before you start the paperwork.

3.title: Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB)
3.body: Full coverage with no annual cap for registered First Nations and recognized Inuit. This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up.

4.heading: Guides worth downloading
4.body: Written by nurses and patient organizations, free, and more thorough than anything on this page.

1.title: Living with an ileostomy, colostomy, or ileal conduit
1.body: Clinician-written patient guides, one per ostomy type, including the less commonly covered ones — jejunostomy, gastrostomy, and gastro-jejunostomy.

2.title: New Ostomy Patient Guide
2.body: American, so the funding sections will not apply here — but the clinical and practical content is excellent and freely available.

3.title: Step Up for Ostomy
3.body: The national awareness and fundraising campaign that anchors the first Saturday of October in Canada.

pharmacist.heading: Fit questions that do not need a waiting room
pharmacist.body: Product fit, restock questions, and everyday concerns — chat with an Ontario pharmacist during business hours (until 5 p.m. Eastern). Olivia helps with shopping anytime; she does not give medical advice.

closing.heading: Living, not managing
closing.body: Most of this stops being a question within a few months. The part that does not — the money, and finding people who have one — is the part most people never find out about, which is the only reason this page needed writing.

this-might-be-you.title: This Might Be You
this-might-be-you.heroBody: What is genuinely different if you are a child’s parent, in your twenties, thinking about pregnancy, or managing this alongside other things in later life.
this-might-be-you.focus: Children and the people raising them, young adults, pregnancy and parenthood, and older adults — what changes for each, and who to ask rather than guess.
this-might-be-you.vibe: Specific, and quick to refer — short on advice, clear on who actually knows.

categoriesIntro.heading: The general advice is not wrong, it is just not enough
categoriesIntro.body: Most ostomy information is written for an average adult who does not exist. These are the situations where the differences are big enough to matter, and where the right move is usually a specific referral rather than a longer article.

1.title: Children, and the people raising them

items.1: A small body has very little fluid in reserve, so a child — especially a baby with an ileostomy — can get dehydrated far faster than an adult losing the same amount. Steady salt loss can also show up as poor weight gain long before anything looks like dehydration, which is why your team may weigh your baby often
items.2: Ask what your child’s normal output is and what counts as too much for their size. Call the same day for output that suddenly rises or turns watery, fewer wet diapers, no tears, a sunken soft spot, unusual sleepiness, or weight that stalls or drops — that is a call to your team, not something to manage with extra fluids at home

items.1: A child’s stoma is not a smaller version of an adult one. They grow, so sizes change constantly — re-measuring is routine rather than occasional
items.2: Pediatric products are a real category rather than repackaged adult stock, shaped smaller and more flexibly for a small abdomen. The adhesive is the part that gets overstated: it is largely the same material as the adult ranges. A baby born at term starts with skin barrier function much like an adult’s, so the extra caution about fragile skin is really for babies born early or at low birth weight, and children who are unwell. The Pouchkins Two-Piece Kit (Flat, 44 mm Green) is the Liivv box for a child’s two-piece supplies — open it below and adjust it with your child’s ostomy nurse before checkout.
items.3: When a pouch keeps lifting, the answer is usually to change it more often rather than to make it stick harder — pediatric barriers are thinner, so they hold up to output for less time. Adhesive removers, barrier films, skin cement and benzoin are generally avoided in infants and young children, because more of any chemical is absorbed through their skin and a stronger bond can tear it on removal. A seal that keeps failing is a call to your child’s ostomy nurse, not a trip for stronger products

3.heading: Two things worth knowing before they happen

items.1: A child’s stoma can prolapse — telescope outward and look alarmingly long. It is more common in children than in adults and usually not an emergency, but colour matters more than length: a stoma that darkens or goes dusky needs an emergency department rather than a phone call, and so does pain, or output that stops
items.2: In a child with an ileostomy, high-fibre foods can cause a blockage, so new foods go in one at a time. Ask your team what each of these looks like for your child, and which number to call after hours

items.1: School needs a written plan rather than a conversation in September: who knows and who backs them up on days they are away, where a spare kit and a full change of clothes live, private washroom access without having to ask in front of the class, and a number the school can call
items.2: Most Canadian schools have no nurse on site, so ask who owns the plan — usually the principal, sometimes a public health nurse — and make sure supply teachers get it. Most schools have never been asked before, so expect to be the one explaining
items.3: Ask the children’s hospital about transition planning a year or two before it happens, and about who the adult service will be. The handoff around seventeen or eighteen is the point at which families most often fall out of specialist care altogether, and it goes better when it is arranged rather than arrived at

1.note: Pediatric ostomy care belongs with a children’s hospital team — the service that created the stoma, working with a nurse who practises in pediatrics. One practical note: “pediatric NSWOC” describes where a nurse works rather than a credential you can search for, and the NSWOCC directory filters by city and by wound, ostomy or continence, with no pediatric option. So the hospital team is the first call, and the one who can point you to the right nurse near you. Coverage for children differs from the adult rules — see Funding & Coverage.

2.title: Being in your twenties with one

items.1: There is no rule about when to tell a partner, and no version of it you owe anyone. Some people say it early so it is out of the way; others wait until someone knows them a bit first
items.2: It often goes fine. It sometimes does not — and if someone decides they cannot be with you because of your stoma, that is information about them rather than a sign you handled it wrong
items.3: Practise it once out loud, with a friend or a peer visitor, before it matters. It is easier the second time

2.heading: Studying and going out

items.1: University accommodations are real and not a favour, but they usually run through two offices: exam arrangements through accessibility services, residence through campus housing, on a separate application. Both want documentation from your care team and both have deadlines that can fall months before term, so ask early — and what is on offer varies, since a private washroom is not something every campus provides
items.2: Alcohol changes output for a lot of people, but the bigger issue is fluid. It is a diuretic, and with an ileostomy you are already losing more water and salt than you used to — dehydration is the most common reason people end up back in hospital after ileostomy surgery. A long night out is still worth planning around rather than avoiding, and if your output is already high, ask your NSWOC or dietitian what your fluid plan should look like first
items.3: Ostomy Canada runs Gutsy Gang social clubs for roughly the 20 to 40 age group, in several cities. Some chapters run the same group under another name, so it is worth asking locally rather than searching only for that one

2.note: Being the only person you know with one is the hardest part for most people this age, and it is the part a peer group fixes fastest.

3.title: Pregnancy and becoming a parent

items.1: If your ostomy is because of IBD, the biggest thing you can influence is where your disease sits when you conceive. Going in while it is quiet is associated with outcomes close to anyone else’s, and conceiving during a flare makes preterm birth and low birth weight more likely
items.2: Start that conversation with your gastroenterologist before you start trying to conceive, rather than after. Some medication decisions take months to settle, and stopping treatment on your own is the thing most likely to go wrong
items.3: Getting pregnant may take longer if you have had pelvic surgery. Pouch surgery in particular is linked to reduced fertility — people with a pelvic pouch are around three times more likely to use IVF — though once they do, their chance of a live birth is the same as anyone else’s. Worth raising early, so that a slow start does not read as an answer

2.heading: While you are pregnant

items.1: People with ostomies do have healthy pregnancies, and a stoma is not a reason not to. It does mean being followed more closely than usual: stoma problems in pregnancy are common rather than rare — blockage and a drop in output are the ones that come up most, and prolapse and parastomal hernia are also reported — and preterm birth is somewhat more likely. Almost all of it is manageable when your team knows to watch for it
items.2: Your abdomen changes shape substantially, so the stoma does too — expect to re-measure often and to change products more than once along the way
items.3: Settle one thing in advance: what counts as an emergency. Blockage is the most common stoma problem in pregnancy, so ask your surgeon or NSWOC now what should make you phone or come in. Get your own threshold and your own number before you need them

2.note: Most of what is known here comes from bowel stomas, so if you have a urostomy or ileal conduit, ask your urologist what is different for you.

items.1: How you deliver is a discussion between you, your obstetric team, your surgical team, and — if your ostomy is because of IBD — your gastroenterologist. Having a stoma does not decide it on its own, but some histories do push toward a planned caesarean, and in practice caesarean rates in people with a stoma run well above average. Ask early which of that applies to you
items.2: If you have an ileal pouch or a continent diversion, say so explicitly. A pouch is not a stoma, and guidelines lean toward a planned caesarean after pouch surgery to protect the sphincter and the pouch’s long-term function. The evidence behind that is not strong and teams do disagree, which is exactly why it belongs in a conversation months ahead rather than one in labour

items.1: The stoma usually settles back toward its pre-pregnancy size over the following weeks, so there is another round of re-measuring and probably another product change on the far side
items.2: Ask about lifting before you are home with a toddler to pick up. Parastomal hernia is the risk being managed, and the advice is specific to your surgery rather than general
items.3: Medication while breastfeeding is a gastroenterologist question if your ostomy is because of IBD. Stopping treatment unilaterally is the common mistake, and it is a phone call to avoid it

3.note: If you are planning a pregnancy, start before you conceive — your gastroenterologist or surgeon, and an NSWOC. If you are already pregnant, tell your obstetric team about your ostomy at the first appointment and ask for an NSWOC to be involved early rather than when something goes wrong.

4.title: Later life, and managing more than one thing

items.1: Dexterity and eyesight. Moldable barriers you shape with your fingers instead of cutting, larger tabs and simpler closures all exist for exactly this. Pre-cut works if your stoma is round and its size has settled; one-piece has fewer steps, while two-piece can be easier to line up by feel. There is no single right answer, so ask an NSWOC to trial a few with you rather than struggling with what you have
items.2: Skin gets thinner and tears more easily with age, and it usually shows up on removal — peel low and slow, pressing the skin away from the barrier rather than pulling the barrier off. Fit still matters just as much, because a barrier that leaks puts output onto skin that is slower to recover. Worth having an NSWOC watch you do a full change
items.3: Managing several conditions at once means more medication, and how much of a pill you absorb depends on your ostomy: with an ileostomy, extended-release and enteric-coated forms can pass through before they have finished working, while a colostomy is closer to normal. Ask a pharmacist to go through the whole list, including anything you buy over the counter

2.heading: What is worth arranging

items.1: Home care and community nursing can help with changes — ask your care team what your province provides rather than assuming there is nothing. Most provinces also fund a pharmacist medication review, and in some, including Ontario, a pharmacist can come to you
items.2: If someone helps you, have them taught by an NSWOC directly — doing a change themselves with the nurse there, not just watching one. Book again if your stoma, your skin, or your products change
items.3: If a move to a retirement residence or long-term care is coming, raise the ostomy before the move rather than after. Staff frequently have no ostomy experience, and the route your supplies arrive by usually changes with the address

2.note: Several provincial programs cover more for seniors, and some are seniors-only — see Funding & Coverage.

5.title: If you are the one helping

items.1: Ask what kind of help is wanted before offering it. Plenty of people want company and logistics, not hands-on care, and being asked is better than being managed
items.2: If you are doing hands-on care, ask an NSWOC to teach you directly — secondhand instructions are how skin problems start
items.3: Caring for someone is tiring in a way people underestimate. Most support groups welcome family and partners, and that is not an imposition on the group

6.title: Where to bring the weight of it

items.1: Ostomy Canada’s Visitor Program puts you in touch with a trained peer visitor who has one themselves. It is support in its own right, not only a way to rehearse a difficult conversation, and it is free
items.2: A local chapter or peer support group is the other standing door, and several run online rather than only in person — worth knowing if you are rural, newly post-operative, or not ready to walk into a room. Listings do go stale, so if the one near you looks dead, Ostomy Canada’s national line is 1-888-969-9698
items.3: Low mood and anxiety are common after ostomy surgery, and they tend to rise in the months afterwards rather than settle. If it is not lifting, that is a reason to say so to your family doctor or surgical team — there is no ostomy-specific counselling service in Canada, so the route runs through your usual primary care and your province’s mental health services

6.note: Nothing here is a substitute for urgent help. If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time.

flat-grant.label: A flat grant, paid to you
flat-grant.blurb: A set amount arrives each year and you buy your own supplies. Anything above the grant is yours to cover — and may be claimable as a medical expense at tax time.

cost-share.label: A percentage cost-share
cost-share.blurb: The program covers a share and you pay the rest, often up to an annual maximum. Low income usually reduces or removes your share.

supplies-in-kind.label: Supplies issued to you
supplies-in-kind.blurb: The program sends the supplies rather than reimbursing you, so you are registered rather than applying — and you do not buy them at retail.

categorical.label: Only if you qualify
categorical.blurb: There is no general program. Coverage runs through specific routes — seniors, social assistance, or a named condition — so the question is which category you fall into.

none.label: No ostomy-specific program
none.blurb: Nothing covers ostomy supplies directly here. Federal routes and tax credits may still help.

ON.name: Ontario
ON.amount: You receive $975 per ostomy per year, paid in two instalments. That rises to $1,300 if you live in a long-term care home or receive social assistance.
ON.howToApply: A physician or nurse practitioner examines you and confirms the ostomy, you both complete form 014-1945-67, and it goes to the Assistive Devices Program. The money is paid to you, not to a vendor, so you can buy supplies wherever you like.
ON.gatekeeper: A physician or nurse practitioner — an NSWOC signature is not required here, which differs from several other provinces.
ON.deadlines: Renew every two years; ADP sends paperwork about three months before expiry. Reviews take up to eight weeks, with the first payment within 30 days of approval.
ON.notes: A temporary ostomy only qualifies if it is needed for longer than six months. If you receive ODSP, the Mandatory Special Necessities benefit can cover costs above the grant — but only once the ADP grant is used up.

BC.name: British Columbia
BC.amount: After an income-based family deductible, PharmaCare pays 70% of eligible costs — 75% if a family member was born before 1940 — then 100% once you reach the family maximum.
BC.howToApply: There is no ostomy application. The step that matters is registering for Fair PharmaCare, which sets your deductible. Register at gov.bc.ca or on 1-800-663-7100, then coverage applies automatically at the till through an authorised provider.
BC.gatekeeper: Nobody clinical — registration and CRA income verification are the gate. The practical gatekeeper is a provider who can bill under a listed product code.
BC.deadlines: Return the mailed consent form within 30 days or registration does not complete. Deductibles run on the calendar year.
BC.notes: If you do not register for Fair PharmaCare you are assigned a $10,000 deductible by default, which means paying for everything yourself. Registering is the single highest-value thing a BC reader can do. Note that skin barriers, protectants, deodorants and cleansers are not covered — people routinely assume they are.

AB.name: Alberta
AB.amount: You pay 25% of the cost, up to a maximum of $500 per family per benefit year — after which AADL covers 100% for the rest of the year. The $500 is a ceiling on what you pay, not an amount you receive.
AB.howToApply: An AADL-approved authoriser assesses you and authorises the products; an approved vendor then bills AADL directly and charges you your share at the point of sale.
AB.gatekeeper: An AADL-approved authoriser — for ostomy products this is a registered nurse, and in practice usually an NSWOC.
AB.deadlines: The benefit year runs 1 July to 30 June.
AB.notes: Low-income Albertans and income-assistance recipients pay nothing at all. If you are excluded because another plan covers you fully — Veterans Affairs, NIHB, or WCB — that other plan is the route.

SK.name: Saskatchewan
SK.amount: The province pays 50% of eligible supplies within quantity limits, and you pay the other half. There is no annual dollar cap.
SK.howToApply: Referral from an ET/NSWOC nurse at a Saskatchewan stoma clinic. This is the only route in — a prescription from your family doctor will not register you, and there is no way to apply for yourself.
SK.gatekeeper: An ET/NSWOC nurse at a provincial stoma clinic. Registration comes before coverage.
SK.notes: Some people get supplies at no charge rather than at 50% — Paraplegia Program registrants, and holders of Supplementary Health Benefits through SAID, SIS or SEI. Worth asking about before assuming you pay half.

MB.name: Manitoba
MB.howToApply: You are registered by an NSWOC after surgery rather than applying yourself. The program then covers basic supplies in full and sends them to you — there is nothing to pay and nothing to claim back.
MB.gatekeeper: An NSWOC, who sets your supply list. Any change to that list also needs NSWOC approval.
MB.deadlines: Order at least two weeks ahead. You can request up to three months of supplies at a time.
MB.notes: There is no dollar figure here, and that is correct rather than missing — limits are set per product in quantities, not in money. Any number you find quoted for Manitoba is not a current benefit rate.

QC.name: Quebec
QC.amount: An annual lump sum of $1,510 for a permanent ostomy, or $1,007 for a temporary one. Paid per ostomy, so two stomas means two allocations.
QC.howToApply: You apply to RAMQ yourself. The only conditions are being insured under the Québec Health Insurance Plan and having had a colostomy, ileostomy or urostomy.
QC.gatekeeper: No clinical sign-off is needed to submit — you apply directly.
QC.deadlines: Amounts are indexed every 1 January. Temporary-ostomy payments are split — half when the application is accepted, then every six months until the stoma is closed.
QC.notes: If you hold a claim slip through social assistance you are reimbursed at actual cost instead of the lump sum. There is also a voluntary agreement that pays your supplier directly and ends the lump-sum payments — useful for some people, but it is a one-way switch worth understanding first.

NB.name: New Brunswick
NB.howToApply: There is no general ostomy program in New Brunswick. If you are a Social Development client with a qualifying health card, eligible supplies cost you nothing and the program pays pharmacies and suppliers directly. If you are not, this route is closed and the federal and tax options below are where to look.
NB.gatekeeper: Your Social Development health card is the gate — it must show the right supplementary or ostomy eligibility code.
NB.notes: Coverage is capped by monthly quantities per product rather than by dollars — for example a set number of wafers and pouches each month.

NS.name: Nova Scotia
NS.amount: Ostomy products are a listed Pharmacare benefit, so what you pay depends on which plan you are in rather than on an ostomy-specific rate.
NS.howToApply: Ostomy products are dispensed as prescriptions through a Nova Scotia pharmacy, so the route is a prescriber plus enrolment in a Pharmacare plan. Family Pharmacare is open to any resident without other drug coverage — worth knowing, because Nova Scotia is often described as having nothing for the general public, and that is not right.
NS.gatekeeper: A physician or nurse practitioner prescribes. An NSWOC is not a gatekeeper here. Plan enrolment is the real step.
NS.deadlines: Reimbursement claims must be submitted within six months of the prescription being dispensed — the most commonly missed deadline in the province.
NS.notes: If you are in active cancer treatment with a combined family income of $35,000 or less, the Boarding, Transportation and Ostomy program reimburses actual supply costs on top. Seniors and Income Assistance clients have their own cost-sharing rules.

PE.name: Prince Edward Island
PE.amount: Reimburses 60% to 100% of what you spend depending on household income, up to $2,400 per full program year.
PE.howToApply: A health care professional submits the Health Care Provider Registration Form for you. After that it is income-tested rather than clinical.
PE.gatekeeper: A health care professional — the program does not specifically require an NSWOC.
PE.deadlines: The program year runs 1 July to 30 June and you must re-apply before it expires or coverage stops. Old invoices are not accepted, so submit regularly rather than saving them up.
PE.notes: Joining part-way through the year pro-rates the maximum.

NL.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
NL.amount: Reimburses 75% of the retail cost of eligible items — but only for 65Plus Plan cardholders, meaning seniors receiving both Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
NL.howToApply: Enrolment happens automatically through your OAS and GIS status. You buy the supplies, keep the original prescription receipts, and claim the 75% back.
NL.gatekeeper: No separate assessor — a prescription and your 65Plus card are what is needed.
NL.notes: If you are under 65, or not receiving GIS, the official page does not name you as eligible for this subsidy. Check the other NLPDP plans and the federal routes below.

YT.name: Yukon
YT.howToApply: Your physician — or a community health nurse where there is no resident doctor — applies on your behalf, and pre-approval before you buy is expected. If you are 65 or over you are covered instead through Seniors Pharmacare, enrolled automatically.
YT.gatekeeper: A physician or community health nurse. Note that having an ostomy is not by itself a qualifying condition — coverage runs through a closed list of chronic diseases, and several common causes of ostomy are not on it. Confirm your specific diagnosis before assuming you are covered.
YT.deadlines: Apply before you buy. Purchases made outside Yukon without prior approval must be claimed within one year.
YT.notes: Yukon publishes no ostomy figure and no deductible amount on its own pages. Numbers circulate elsewhere; we are not repeating them, because we could not confirm them. Call the program to get your own numbers before planning around them.

NT.name: Northwest Territories
NT.amount: Seniors 60+ and lower-income bands pay nothing. Higher bands pay 25% of the cost up to a yearly family maximum of $500 to $1,500 depending on income band, after which the plan pays everything. There is no deductible on medical supplies.
NT.howToApply: Register under the Extended Health Benefits policy, which involves an income assessment — unless you are 60 or over, in which case you are enrolled on age. A prescriber then orders the supplies.
NT.gatekeeper: Program registration plus a prescription from a recognised health care prescriber.
NT.deadlines: Bands and maximums reset on 1 September.
NT.notes: Ostomy supplies are covered under general medical supplies rather than a named ostomy benefit. First Nations and Inuit residents go through NIHB instead.

NU.name: Nunavut
NU.howToApply: There is no ostomy-specific program. If you qualify under specified conditions or seniors coverage, prescribed medical supplies are covered including fitting and shipping — which matters a great deal in Nunavut. Most Nunavummiut are Inuit and are covered federally through NIHB instead.
NU.gatekeeper: A prescription is required either way.
NU.notes: Nunavut publishes no amount, cap, or per-item rate for supplies, and no list we could confirm of which conditions qualify. Call Extended Health Benefits on 867-645-8029 to ask whether your diagnosis is on the list rather than assuming either way.

1.q: How often should I empty or change my ostomy pouch?
1.a: Empty drainable pouches at around one-third to one-half full. Full system changes are often every few days, or sooner if you feel burning, itching, or a leak. Your NSWOC can help you find a wear time that suits your body — wear time varies a great deal between people and is not something to judge yourself against.

2.q: Can I customize an ostomy kit?
2.a: Yes. Start from a curated kit, adjust the quantities, add anything that was missing, and save your version — or subscribe so the restock keeps arriving on your own schedule.

3.q: How do ostomy supply subscriptions work?
3.a: On a product page, choose Subscribe & save, pick a frequency that matches your wear time, then check out like any order. Skip a delivery when you still have extras — no charge, nothing ships. Manage pause, skip, or cancel under Account → Subscriptions.

4.q: What belongs in an ostomy go-bag?
4.a: A spare barrier and pouch, soft wipes, disposal bags, and any skin protectant or adhesive remover you use — plus spare underwear or a liner if that helps you feel ready to be out.

5.q: What can I ask a pharmacist about my ostomy?
5.a: Everyday product and restock questions, in Ontario during business hours until 5 p.m. Eastern. Clinical concerns — fit, skin, and anything about the stoma itself — belong with your NSWOC or surgeon rather than a pharmacist.

fundingPage.dtcNote: The most valuable and most misunderstood item on this page — and the one people most often get refused.
fundingPage.dtcPoint1: Having an ostomy does not qualify you on its own. This is the part almost every summary gets wrong. A well-managed routine is frequently refused, and the CRA’s own guidance says so.
fundingPage.dtcPoint2: The test: you are unable to manage bowel or bladder function, or it takes you roughly three times longer than someone of similar age without the impairment, at least 90% of the time, for a continuous 12 months — assessed with your appliances and routine already in place.
fundingPage.dtcPoint3: So what gets approved is complications and time burden, not the stoma itself. Leaks, skin breakdown, repeated changes, night-time management, time lost from work — that is what belongs on the form.
fundingPage.dtcPoint4: Apply through the eliminating category — bowel or bladder function — not life-sustaining therapy. Only a medical doctor or nurse practitioner can certify it. Your NSWOC can help you describe your routine accurately, but cannot sign the form.
fundingPage.dtcPoint5: It is still worth applying: approval can be backdated up to ten years, and it unlocks the RDSP and the Canada Disability Benefit. A refusal costs you those too, which is why the wording matters so much.
fundingPage.dtcPoint6: If you are refused, the medical expense claim below needs no approval at all.
fundingPage.nihbPoint1: For registered First Nations and recognized Inuit, NIHB covers approved ostomy items subject to quantity limits and prior approval. Recognized providers bill NIHB directly, so there is no upfront cost to you.
fundingPage.nihbPoint2: This replaces the provincial route rather than topping it up — so start here rather than applying to your province first.
fundingPage.nihbPoint3: There is an exception process for quantities or items outside the standard list. High output is a common and legitimate reason to use it.
fundingPage.expensesHeading: Medical expenses on your tax return
fundingPage.expensesPoint1: Whatever your province does not cover may be claimable. Several provinces say so explicitly on their own program pages.
fundingPage.expensesPoint2: Keep receipts, including shipping where it is not covered.
fundingPage.ranOutHeading: The funding ran out before the year did
fundingPage.ranOut1Body: Often the fastest win is not more money but a better fit — fewer changes, longer wear time, less waste. An NSWOC can also tell you what actually gets approved in your region.
fundingPage.ranOut2Body: Hollister, Coloplast, and Convatec all run free support lines with samples and nurse access, regardless of where you buy. They will also help you navigate coverage.
fundingPage.ranOut3Heading: Check social assistance and disability routes
fundingPage.ranOut3Body: Provincial disability and social assistance programs sometimes top up ostomy coverage above the standard grant. This is worth asking about directly.
fundingPage.ranOut4Body: Ostomy Canada chapters know the local landscape, and some hold donated supplies. Treat second-hand product carefully — check the expiry date, that the inner packaging is unopened, that the size matches what you use, and ask how it was stored.
fundingPage.movingIntro: Nobody writes this down, and it catches people out. Moving resets your coverage entirely — different model, different amount, different forms, and often a different person who has to sign them.
fundingPage.before1: Claim anything outstanding — most programs will not pay across a move.
fundingPage.before2: Ask your NSWOC for a written summary of your current setup, sizes, and products. It shortens registration at the other end considerably.
fundingPage.before3: Stock up enough to cover the gap while new coverage is approved.
fundingPage.arrive1: Find an NSWOC early — in several provinces you cannot register at all without one.
fundingPage.arrive2: Check the new province’s model above. If you move from a grant province to a supplies-in-kind one, you stop buying at retail entirely.
fundingPage.arrive3: Expect a waiting period, and budget for it.
fundingPage.closingHeading: Money should not be the reason you ration supplies
fundingPage.closingBody: If the numbers are not working, that is worth saying out loud to your care team. There are usually more routes than people realise.

faq.note: Practical notes, not medical advice. Each answer lists where it comes from.

1.q: Can I order my supplies here, and will my plan pay?
1.a: You can order diabetes supplies such as meters, strips, lancets, pen needles, sensors and pump supplies from the shelf. Liivv’s pharmacies serve all of Canada, Quebec and the territories included, but insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec. To fill a prescription, send it from <link>your account’s Pharmacy page</link>: choose Add prescription, then transfer it from your current pharmacy or ask your doctor to fax it. What’s covered for pumps, sensors, strips and needles is different in each province and territory, and Diabetes Canada <link>compares them by province and territory</link>. Coverage changes, so check the date on each comparison and confirm with your provincial or territorial plan. Our pharmacy in your province bills your provincial drug plan directly for what it covers, except in Quebec, where orders are paid for privately. Other programs each pay their own way: where one pays you back, we can give you an invoice for your claim. Check how yours pays before you order, or ask the CDEs at Bayshore Express Pharmacy.

2.a: On Diabetes Care pages, on diabetes product pages, and in a cart with diabetes supplies, we turn off advertising signals. What you read and buy there isn’t used for ads or to build ad audiences. The page address and title are left out of our site analytics, and so are the names of diabetes products.

3.q: What if a sensor stops working or comes off early?
3.a: Diabetes Canada says a sensor can be up to 15 minutes slower than a finger-prick check to show your blood sugar, and advises keeping a meter and strips as a backup. So keep them where you can reach them. The Certified Diabetes Educators at <link>Bayshore Express Pharmacy</link> can help with sensor and supply questions: <link>call 1-844-561-1254</link> or <link>email BayshoreExpress@bayshore.ca</link>, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, except holidays. If someone can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure, <link>call 911</link>. For a low, a high or a sick day, go to <link>Staying Safe</link>.

4.q: Where do used needles, lancets and sensor applicators go?
4.a: Into a sharps container. In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the Health Products Stewardship Association (HPSA) gives out free sharps containers at participating collection locations, such as pharmacies. When yours is full, seal it and return it to a drop-off location. Its program takes lancets, pen tips (pen needles), syringes, infusion sets and sensor (CGM) applicators with needles. It doesn’t take glucose meters. HPSA says never to put used sharps in the garbage or the recycling. Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy: Diabetes Canada says many pharmacies supply safe, puncture-proof containers.

5.a: Yes. Insulin is listed in the shop. A pharmacist reviews and dispenses every insulin and glucagon order, shipped in plain packaging. Insulin is shipped cold-chain. fundingPage.payingIntro: Some programs pay a pharmacy or a supplier. Others pay you back, or pay you a set amount. Here’s how that works when you order from us.
fundingPage.directBody: Our pharmacy in your province bills your provincial drug plan directly for what the plan covers. Each Liivv pharmacy is enrolled with its own province’s plan:
fundingPage.directQuebec: Not in Quebec: Quebec’s public drug plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec, so orders shipped to Quebec are paid for privately. Insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec.
fundingPage.directOther: Federal programs, territorial plans and private insurers aren’t on this list. For those, check how each one pays, or ask us.
fundingPage.claimBody: Some programs pay you back when you send them a receipt. Some pay you a set amount instead: Ontario’s Assistive Devices Program pays up to $2,400 a year toward pump supplies, sent to you as $600 every 3 months, and you buy the supplies yourself. Others pay only a pharmacy or supplier directly, so a receipt from us won’t work for them.
fundingPage.claimCheck: Paying for an order yourself and claiming it back? Ask us for an invoice for your claim. We can’t promise that a program will accept a claim, so check its rules before you order.
fundingPage.payLaterBody: For insulin pump supplies, Omnipod pods included, you can pay after you receive your order instead of when you place it. Our customer service team checks that you’re eligible first.

payLaterTerms.1: Start with three orders in a row, paid as usual.
payLaterTerms.2: Then accept the program’s terms with a $1.00 authorization on your credit card. There’s no credit check.
payLaterTerms.3: Pay for each order within 45 days of receiving it, or with your next order, whichever comes first.
payLaterTerms.4: Omnipod pod orders are billed to your card every 90 days.
payLaterTerms.5: If your card is declined, we try it 3 more times. After that, the balance is due within 3 business days. Prepaid cards can’t be used.
payLaterTerms.6: A late payment can hold up your next shipment and end your place in the program.
