categoriesIntro.heading: You don’t have to learn it all at once
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter covers the first days after a diagnosis, then getting set up. If you’ve just been told, start at the top. If you already have a plan and supplies, start at Do I need a meter?

startHere.heading: Just been told, or setting up?

1.title: Just been told

items.1: There’s no right way to feel about this news, and no need to take it all in at once
items.2: Diabetes Canada says depression is more common in people with diabetes, so looking after your mood is part of looking after your diabetes
items.3: Diabetes Canada’s guideline says diabetes teams should ask everyone, from time to time, about diabetes distress and about mood and anxiety. You can bring it up first
items.4: Your team will start with what you need to know first. The rest can wait

1.note: If it isn’t easing, tell your diabetes team or your doctor. If you’d like to talk to a mental health professional, Breakthrough T1D keeps a Mental Health + Diabetes Directory of registered providers.

figure.body: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.

1.prompt: If it isn’t easing, or it’s hard to get through the day

2.prompt: If you’d like to talk to a mental health professional
2.detail: Breakthrough T1D keeps a Mental Health + Diabetes Directory of registered mental health providers.

2.title: Which diabetes is this?

items.1: Type 1: the pancreas doesn’t make insulin. Diabetes Canada says 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1, and it can start in adulthood too
items.2: Type 2: the most common type, 90 to 95% of people with diabetes. It may have no symptoms
items.3: Gestational diabetes: shows up during pregnancy, in 3 to 20% of pregnancies. It usually goes away after the birth, but it raises the chance of type 2 later, for you and your child
items.4: Prediabetes: blood sugar that’s higher than normal, but not yet high enough to be called type 2 diabetes
items.5: Less common types: Diabetes Canada’s guideline lists less common forms, such as LADA (which it counts as type 1) and monogenic diabetes, and says some cases are hard to classify. If your type doesn’t seem to fit, ask your team

2.note: Know Your Type has a card for each one, including the less common types.

3.title: Your target ranges

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s usual targets are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after eating
items.2: If your A1C isn’t at target, your team may set a lower after-meal target, weighing it against the risk of lows. Diabetes Canada gives 5.0 to 8.0
items.3: A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. It’s usually done about every 3 months, and Diabetes Canada’s usual target is 7.0% or less
items.4: If you use a sensor, Diabetes Canada’s guideline uses international targets: for most adults, more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0
items.5: Your team may set different targets, for example for children, or if you’re pregnant, frail, or often have severe lows

3.note: Write your own targets on the card and keep it with your meter. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.

ruler.heading: Diabetes Canada’s usual targets, in mmol/L
ruler.lowLink: What to do about a low: The Rule of 15
ruler.teamNote: Your team may set different numbers, for example for a child. Use theirs.

fields.4: Time in range, if I use a sensor

4.title: Food and movement: first steps

items.1: Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant protein more often
items.2: It suggests water as your drink of choice, and limiting highly processed foods
items.3: Diabetes Canada’s guideline supports more than one way of eating, including Mediterranean, DASH and vegetarian. A dietitian can help you find what fits
items.4: Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes of activity a day, and build up
items.5: Diabetes Canada suggests working up to 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity, such as 30 minutes on 5 days
items.6: If you haven’t been active for a while, talk to your doctor before you start anything harder than a brisk walk
items.7: If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active

4.note: Carb counting, eating out and more on moving your body are in Everyday Liivving. If you take insulin, ask your team how to plan around activity.

5.title: Supporting someone newly diagnosed

items.1: Ask what help they’d like. Some people want company at appointments, and some would rather manage on their own
items.2: Learn what a low looks like for them, and where they keep fast-acting sugar. The steps are in <link>The Rule of 15</link>, in Staying Safe
items.3: If they’re at risk of a severe low, such as people who take insulin, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says the people around them should be taught to call 911, and how to give glucagon. The signs that need emergency care are in Staying Safe
items.4: If they have type 1, immediate family aged 2 to 45, and other relatives aged 2 to 20, can ask about free research screening through TrialNet, anywhere in Canada. The details are in <link>Type 1 starts before symptoms</link>, in Know Your Type
items.5: Your own feelings count too. If you’re caring for a child or teen with type 1, Breakthrough T1D has a Caregiver Guide

5.note: More for families and caregivers is in This Might Be You.

2.heading: If they’re at risk of a severe low

6.title: Do I need a meter?

items.1: Whether you check your blood sugar at home, and how often, depends on your type and your treatment. Your team will tell you what you need
items.2: If you take insulin more than once a day, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says to check at least 3 times a day
items.3: For type 1 on injections or a pump, Diabetes Canada’s guidelines recommend a sensor that reads all the time (a continuous glucose monitor). Ask your team whether that fits you
items.4: A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar, so Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter and strips as a backup
items.5: Choosing a meter, and the strips and lancets that go with it, is in Your Tools

6.note: Some provinces cover strips and sensors, and how much often depends on your treatment. <link>Funding & Coverage</link> has the details for your province.

7.title: Your medicines and your pharmacist

items.1: What is each of my medicines for, and when do I take it?
items.2: Can any of them cause a low? If so, what should I keep with me?
items.3: Do any of them need to be paused on a sick day? Diabetes Canada’s sick-day sheet has a space for your pharmacist to write this down
items.4: How do I store each one, and how long does it keep once it’s open?
items.5: Which supplies go with my medicines, and are they covered by my plan?

7.note: Take this list to your pharmacist or your next appointment, with your medicines or a list of them. Your prescriber chooses your medicines. Your pharmacist helps you use them safely.

8.title: Starting insulin

items.1: Diabetes Canada says everyone with type 1, and many people with type 2, need insulin to stay healthy
items.2: There’s no one-size-fits-all plan. Your team works out with you how many injections, when, how much, and whether a pump suits you
items.3: Insulin can be taken with a pen, a syringe or a pump. Pens come with an instruction book, so read it to learn how yours works
items.4: Change where you inject each time. Diabetes Canada says this helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly
items.5: Use a new pen tip or needle every time, then put it in a sharps container
items.6: Insulin raises your risk of a low. Diabetes Canada says to always have fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out. The steps are in <link>The Rule of 15</link>, in Staying Safe
items.7: Storage is different for each insulin. Follow the leaflet that came with yours, or ask your pharmacist
items.8: Diabetes Canada says to throw out insulin that has been frozen, has been in temperatures over 30°C, or has expired

8.note: Your prescriber chooses your insulin, and fine-tuning your routine takes time. A step-by-step injection guide is in Your Tools.

9.title: Sharps from day one

items.1: Used lancets, pen tips and needles go in a sharps container. Diabetes Canada says pen tips and needles are for one use only
items.2: Sharps include lancets, pen needles, sensor applicators that have a needle, infusion sets and syringes
items.3: Never put used sharps in the garbage or recycling, says the Health Products Stewardship Association
items.4: In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, participating pharmacies give out free sharps containers and take them back
items.5: Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy. Diabetes Canada says many pharmacies supply containers and swap a full one for a new one

9.note: Ask your pharmacy where to return a full container near you.

10.title: Your starter supply list

items.1: If you check with a meter: the meter, its strips and lancets, and a sharps container
items.2: If you take insulin: a new pen tip or needle for each injection, and a sharps container
items.3: If you take insulin: fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out
items.4: A card in your wallet that says you have diabetes, or medical ID such as a bracelet or necklace
items.5: If you use a sensor: a meter and strips as a backup
items.6: If you use a pump: backup insulin pens or syringes, extra pump supplies, ketone strips or a blood ketone meter, and a written copy of your pump settings

10.note: Your team’s list comes first. Ask them whether you need ketone strips or glucagon.

11.title: Who to ask

items.1: Your diabetes educator: your plan, your readings and everyday questions. Many are Certified Diabetes Educators (CDE®), licensed health professionals certified in diabetes education
items.2: Your doctor: your diagnosis, your prescriptions and your checkups
items.3: A pharmacist: what each medicine is for, how to store it, and your sick-day medicine plan
items.4: How you’re feeling: your team, or a registered mental health provider from Breakthrough T1D’s Mental Health + Diabetes Directory

11.note: Not sure where to start? Start with your diabetes educator. Some educators in the CDE directory see people without a referral.

1.heading: Learning the basics
1.body: The first months are for learning, at your own pace. Your diabetes educator can go over your plan, your readings and your questions. With gestational diabetes or prediabetes, your checkups are different, so ask your team which of these apply.

2.heading: About every 3 months: A1C
2.body: Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests an A1C test about every 3 months. For adults whose numbers have been steady at target, your team may space it out. Your usual target is in Your target ranges.

3.heading: Eyes
3.body: Diabetes Canada says to have an eye exam once a year, unless your eye-care professional suggests something different. With type 2, the first one is at diagnosis. With type 1, for people 15 and over, they start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule. Your team tells you when yours is due.

4.heading: Kidneys
4.body: Diabetes Canada’s guideline says two tests, called ACR and eGFR, check your kidneys at least once a year. With type 2 they start at diagnosis. With type 1 they usually start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule, so ask your team.

5.heading: Feet
5.body: Diabetes Canada suggests washing, drying and checking your feet every day, with a mirror if you need one. At least once a year, your team checks your bare feet, including feeling and blood flow.

staying-safe.heroBody: Lows, highs, ketones and sick days: what to check, what to do, and when to call. Short enough to use in a hurry.

categoriesIntro.heading: Your plan, in one place
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter helps you follow the plan your diabetes team made with you, and shows when it’s time to call. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.

urgent.heading: Get emergency care now
urgent.intro: Everyday lows and highs follow your plan. These don’t. Get emergency care now if the person:
urgent.action: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

signs.1: Can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Call 911, give glucagon if you have it, turn them on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth
signs.2: Is vomiting and can’t keep fluids down
signs.3: Has blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L, or large ketones in their urine (ranges written for type 1 diabetes)
signs.4: Has deep or hard breathing or fruity-smelling breath, or is very sleepy or confused with a high blood sugar or ketones. In pregnancy, or with some diabetes medicines, DKA can happen even when blood sugar is near normal

startHere.heading: Is your number low, or high?

1.title: Know your low

items.1: Diabetes Canada calls a blood sugar below 3.9 mmol/L low
items.2: Level 1: below 3.9, down to 3.0
items.3: Level 2: below 3.0
items.4: Level 3: a low at any number where you need someone else’s help to treat it
items.5: If you use a sensor, Canadian targets for most people aim for less than 4% of the day below 3.9

1.note: Some Canadian guidance for driving and for school uses 4.0 instead of 3.9. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.

2.title: The Rule of 15

items.1: Take 15 g of fast-acting sugar
items.2: Wait 15 minutes, then check your blood sugar again
items.3: If it’s still below 3.9, take another 15 g
items.4: Once it’s back up, if your next meal is more than an hour away, have a snack with a starch and a protein

2.note: After a low, anyone who drives, teens included, should wait at least 40 minutes, and until their blood sugar is at least 5.0, before driving. More on driving in Everyday Liivving.

figure.optionsHeading: 15 g of fast-acting sugar is one of these:

options.1: Glucose tablets that add up to 15 g
options.2: ⅔ cup (150 mL) of juice or regular pop
options.4: 1 tablespoon of sugar dissolved in water

figure.childNote: From Diabetes Canada’s guideline for children with type 1 diabetes who use injections, or a pump that doesn’t adjust insulin on its own. Children on an automated (closed-loop) system may need less. If your child has another type of diabetes, or uses an automated system, ask their team how much to give.

childSteps.1: Give the amount for their age
childSteps.4: Still below 3.9? Give that amount again

childItems.1: Give fast-acting sugar. The amount for the child’s age is in the table
childItems.2: Wait 15 minutes, then check their blood sugar again
childItems.3: If it’s still below 3.9, give the amount in the table again
childItems.4: Once it’s back up, if their next meal is more than an hour away, give them a snack with a starch and a protein

figure.childOptionsNote: Honey isn’t on the list for children. Health Canada says not to give any honey to babies under 1 year.
figure.aidNote: On an automated (closed-loop) insulin system? Diabetes Canada’s type 1 guideline says people of any age may treat a low they can manage themselves with less, 5 to 10 g. Ask your team what to use.

3.title: Glucagon: help someone else gives

items.1: Glucagon is for a low when the person can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Someone else gives it
items.2: It comes as a nasal spray or an injection. Your pharmacist can tell you which is available
items.3: Call 911, or have someone call. Give glucagon, turn the person on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth
items.4: If a low is affecting the person’s thinking or movement but they can still swallow, Diabetes Canada’s sheet says to give 20 g of fast-acting sugar
items.5: At school, staff named in the student’s care plan, and trained, give glucagon when the plan includes consent for it

3.note: Ask your pharmacist to show you how your glucagon works, and check its expiry date from time to time. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep.

4.title: Lows that sneak up

items.1: Exercise can keep lowering your blood sugar for up to 48 hours afterwards
items.2: Check your blood sugar regularly, especially if you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar
items.3: If you take insulin or some diabetes pills, alcohol can cause a low up to 24 hours after you drink
items.4: Diabetes Canada suggests eating carbohydrate when you drink, and checking your blood sugar before bed
items.5: Make sure someone with you knows to call 911 if you pass out, and to give you glucagon if you have it. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says glucagon may not work as well if you’ve had more than 2 standard drinks in the past few hours, so the 911 call matters even more
items.6: A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar. Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter as a backup

4.note: Ask your team how to plan your medicines around exercise and drinking.

items.1: Carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active
items.2: If you have glucagon, show the people you spend time with how it works. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says they should be taught
items.3: Wear medical ID, such as a bracelet or necklace
items.4: For a child at school, a care plan made before the school year covers daily care and emergencies, with at least two trained staff
items.5: Diabetes@School says to treat a student’s low right away, where it happens, and not to leave them alone
items.6: Students may carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar

6.title: Highs

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s usual targets are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after meals. Your team may set different ones
items.2: Symptoms of a high can show up when your fasting blood sugar is 11 or higher
items.3: If your blood sugar stays above 14 before meals for more than a few meals, check for ketones
items.4: Ketones can build up even when blood sugar is close to normal, for example in pregnancy or with a type of diabetes pill called an SGLT2 inhibitor. Ask your pharmacist whether any of your pills is, or contains, one

6.note: Very high blood sugar or high ketones need care right away. The signs are at the top of this page.

7.title: Ketones: check and act

items.1: Ketones build up when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy
items.2: You can check ketones in your blood or in your urine. Your team will tell you which to use
items.3: Check when your blood sugar stays high. With type 1, check when you’re sick too, especially with vomiting, stomach pain or a fever. With other types, check when you’re sick if your team has told you to
items.4: Diabetes Canada’s guideline for type 1 diabetes says to put off hard exercise if blood ketones are 1.5 or higher
items.5: Signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) include thirst, passing a lot of urine, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, deeper breathing, fruity-smelling breath, and feeling tired, sleepy or confused. DKA needs medical care right away

7.note: The ladder below is adapted from Breakthrough T1D and was written for type 1 diabetes. If you have another type, ask your team which numbers to use. With any type, Diabetes Canada says high ketones need medical care right away.

8.title: Sick days

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s sick-day sheet is for vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or a lot of heat or humidity without enough to drink: anything that can leave you dehydrated

2.heading: What the sheet says to do

items.1: Drink plenty of fluids with little sugar, unless you’ve been told to limit fluids
items.2: If you can’t eat, the sheet lists foods with 15 g of carbohydrate to have instead
items.3: Diabetes Canada says that if you use insulin, you should keep taking it when you’re sick. Check your blood sugar more often. The sheet says your insulin may need adjusting, so ask your team how

items.1: The sheet lists some medicines to stop for a short time if you’re eating less, or dehydrated, for more than 24 hours
items.2: Which of your own medicines this means is a question for your pharmacist. The sheet has a space for them to write it down
items.3: The sheet says to restart them once you’re eating and drinking normally

items.1: Vomiting and can’t keep fluids down: go to the emergency department. If you can reach your team right away, call them too
items.2: If you’re sick and can’t eat, call your doctor or go to the emergency department if you vomit or have diarrhea 2 or more times in 4 hours
items.3: Call your team or go to the emergency department if you can’t drink enough, don’t know which medicines to stop or how to adjust your insulin, or your ketones are moderate. Large ketones need emergency care now
items.4: Do the same if vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, passing a lot of urine, extreme thirst, weakness or fever isn’t getting better. Trouble breathing needs emergency care now

8.note: Fill in the plan on this card with your pharmacist and diabetes team before you’re sick, so it’s ready when you need it.

fields.2: How often to check my blood sugar when I’m sick
fields.3: When to check ketones, and blood or urine
fields.4: My medicines to pause, and when to restart them (filled in with my pharmacist)
fields.5: Foods and drinks I can manage when I’m sick

9.title: On a pump: an unexplained high

items.1: Diabetes Canada suggests keeping backup supplies, such as rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, and learning how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump
items.2: If your blood sugar is high and you can’t explain it, check your ketones and follow the ladder in Ketones: check and act
items.3: Keep a written copy of your pump settings in your emergency kit

9.note: Your pump team’s plan comes first. Ask them what to do if you think your pump has stopped giving insulin.

items.1: Diabetes Canada suggests an emergency kit with at least one to two weeks of supplies
items.2: Include fast-acting sugar, glucagon if you have it, ketone strips and a sharps container
items.3: If you use a pump, add a written copy of your settings
items.4: Diabète Québec says to keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C. Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired
items.5: How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Diabète Québec says most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin

items.1: 911: someone can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure
items.2: Emergency department, or 911: blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA such as deep breathing or fruity-smelling breath
items.3: Your diabetes team, now: blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones. If you can’t reach them, go to the emergency department
items.4: Your diabetes team: blood ketones 0.6 to under 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones
items.5: Your pharmacist: your sick-day medicine plan, and how your glucagon works

categoriesIntro.heading: The right supplies, used well
categoriesIntro.body: This chapter explains your tools and how to use them. It doesn’t choose your treatment: your team does that with you. If your team, or the guide that came with your device, says something different, follow them.

startHere.heading: Checking your glucose, or getting insulin in?

1.title: Choosing a meter

items.1: A meter reads a drop of blood from a finger prick. The drop goes on a test strip, and the strip goes into the meter
items.2: You can get a meter at most pharmacies, or from your diabetes educator
items.3: Once you have a meter, get trained on it before you start using it
items.4: How often you check depends on your treatment plan. Your team will tell you when, and how often
items.5: Even if you use a sensor, Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter and strips, to double-check a reading and as a backup

1.note: Ask your pharmacist or educator which meter suits you. Coverage is under How supplies get paid for, below.

2.title: Strips, lancets and control solution that match

items.1: Diabetes Canada suggests asking which test strips to use with your meter, and whether your meter needs to be coded to read them
items.2: Used lancets go in a sharps container. Many pharmacies give out puncture-proof containers and swap a full one for a new one
items.3: In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the Health Products Stewardship Association (HPSA) gives out free sharps containers at participating collection locations, such as pharmacies
items.4: HPSA says never to put sharps in the garbage or the recycling
items.5: Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy how to return used sharps

4.title: Sensors: which pairs with what

items.1: A sensor sits on your skin like a small patch, held on by adhesive, with a thin filament just under the skin. It measures sugar in the fluid between your cells, so it can read your sugar without a finger prick each time
items.2: Some sensors give a reading only when you scan them with your phone. Others show your sugar all the time and can sound alarms for lows and highs
items.3: Some sensors connect to an insulin pump. That connection is what a hybrid closed-loop system needs
items.4: Diabetes Canada says this technology isn’t for everyone, and suggests talking with your team about whether it’s right for you

4.note: Makers update which devices work together. Before you switch a sensor or a pump, check with your team, your device maker or a Liivv pharmacist who is a Certified Diabetes Educator (CDE).

5.title: Wearing a sensor, and time in range

items.1: Time in range is the share of your day that your sugar stays in your target range
items.2: For most people, Diabetes Canada’s guideline aims for more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0 mmol/L
items.3: It also aims for less than 4% of the day below 3.9
items.4: Breakthrough T1D says going from 60% to 65% of the day in range adds about an hour a day in range
items.5: Targets can be different in pregnancy, and for children, older adults and people who have lows often. Your team sets yours
items.6: You can share your sensor readings from your phone with your diabetes team, so they can see your patterns over time
items.7: A sensor and a finger check are more likely to differ when you’re eating or exercising. If how you feel doesn’t match your sensor, or you’re treating a low, a finger check gives the most accurate number

5.note: Some Diabetes Canada pages give the range as 4.0 to 10.0. If your team gave you a range, use theirs.

7.title: Pen needles: length and angle

items.1: An insulin pen comes filled with insulin. You put a new needle tip on for each injection
items.2: You need a separate pen for each type of insulin you use
items.3: Diabetes Canada suggests shorter, thinner needles. Diabète Québec suggests 4, 5 or 6 mm, so the insulin doesn’t go into muscle
items.4: For adults, Diabète Québec says a skin lift may not be needed with a 4 mm needle, and to use one with a needle 8 mm or longer
items.5: Diabetes Canada says to put the needle in at 90°, with a quick, smooth motion. With a longer needle, 8 or 12 mm, you may need to gently lift the skin, or go in at 45°
items.6: If there’s little fat on your arms, legs or belly, Diabète Québec says a skin lift may be needed even with a 5 or 6 mm needle

7.note: Your educator or pharmacist can show you which length suits you, and how to lift the skin if you need to.

8.title: Syringes, and insulin strength

items.1: Today’s syringes are smaller and use thinner needles. They cost less than pens and pumps
items.2: Insulin comes in more than one strength. Most is U-100 (100 units/mL). Some insulins are stronger, such as U-200, U-300, U-500 or U-700, and each of these comes in its own pen
items.3: If you use a pump, Diabetes Canada suggests keeping rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes as a backup
items.4: Flying? The Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA) says a syringe needs its needle guard on, and the insulin it’s for has to be with you
items.5: If your insulin is stronger than U-100 (the label says 200, 300, 500 or 700 units/mL), never use a syringe to take it out of the pen. A syringe can’t measure it correctly, and you could get far too much insulin and a severe low

8.note: Always carry a spare pen and needles. If your pen stops working, or you can’t use it, ask your pharmacist what to do before you use a syringe.

9.title: Giving an injection, step by step

items.1: Wash your hands with soap and water, and make sure the injection site is clean
items.2: You don’t need to wipe your skin with alcohol. If you do, let it dry completely first
items.3: Check the expiry date on your cartridge or vial
items.4: Wipe the rubber seal on the pen or vial with alcohol before you put on a new needle. Don’t wipe the needle itself
items.5: Cloudy insulin needs mixing until it looks milky white: roll it 10 times between your hands, then tip it upside down and back 10 times. Don’t shake it

items.1: Put on a new needle, then prime the pen to check the needle isn’t blocked, the way your pen’s instructions say
items.2: Dial the dose your team has set
items.3: Put the needle in at 90° with a quick, smooth motion
items.4: Press the button until the counter shows 0, or the syringe is empty. Count to 10 before you take the needle out
items.5: Put the needle straight into your sharps container. Don’t leave a needle on your pen between injections
items.6: Don’t inject through clothing

9.note: Your pen comes with an instruction book. Diabetes Canada suggests reading it, so you know how your pen works.

10.title: Choosing and moving your sites

items.1: Change where you inject each time. Diabetes Canada says this helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly
items.2: Insulin goes in fastest and most evenly from the belly. Stay about 5 cm (2 inches), three finger widths, from your belly button
items.3: Insulin goes in more slowly from the buttocks and thighs. The back of the upper arm is hard to reach on your own, so it’s often not suggested
items.4: Diabète Québec suggests leaving at least 1 to 2 cm, about a finger width, between injections, and splitting each area into four zones, using one zone for a week before you move on
items.5: Check and feel your injection areas regularly for lumps or dents
items.6: Avoid scars, moles and any other changes in the skin
items.7: Diabète Québec says injecting into a part of your body you’re about to exercise can make insulin act faster and lower your sugar

10.note: If you find a lump or a dent, show it to your educator or your team.

items.1: Diabète Québec says to keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C
items.2: Keep the insulin you’re using at room temperature
items.3: Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired
items.4: How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Diabète Québec says most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin

items.6: Diabetes Canada says insulin goes in your carry-on when you fly, not in checked luggage
items.7: CATSA lets insulin, juice and gels through security above the 100 mL limit, but you need to declare them separately

12.title: Pumps and automated insulin delivery, in plain words

items.1: An insulin pump is a small device worn outside your body. It gives insulin through a small tube under the skin, 24 hours a day
items.2: It gives a small, steady trickle of insulin between meals and overnight. Extra doses can be given when they’re needed, for food or to bring a high down
items.3: Some pumps connect to a sensor and respond to your readings. Diabetes Canada calls this a hybrid closed-loop system. You may also hear it called automated insulin delivery
items.4: For type 1 diabetes, Diabetes Canada’s guideline prefers automated insulin delivery for everyone who is willing and able to wear and use the devices
items.5: Your team works with you to decide whether a pump suits you, and on your pump settings

14.title: Pump backup and set changes

items.1: Diabetes Canada suggests making a pump backup plan before you need one
items.2: Backup supplies include rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, long-acting insulin if your team says you need it, extra infusion sets and reservoirs, and ketone strips or a blood ketone meter
items.3: Learn how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump, and keep a written copy of your pump settings

categoriesIntro.heading: Diabetes, around the rest of your life
categoriesIntro.body: The first half is the everyday: what you eat, how you move, how you feel, and getting around. The second is the checkups that find changes early. If your team gave you different targets or advice, use theirs.

1.title: Food without a rulebook

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s guideline describes several styles of eating that work well with diabetes, including Mediterranean, Nordic, DASH and vegetarian
items.2: Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with protein from plants more often
items.3: Make water your drink of choice
items.4: Choose whole and less processed foods more often than sugary drinks, fast food and refined grains
items.5: Notice when you’re hungry and when you’re full
items.6: Culture and food traditions can be part of healthy eating

1.note: A registered dietitian can help you make a meal plan that fits your culture, your tastes and your blood sugar goals.

2.title: Carb counting

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests learning to count carbohydrate, because how much you eat at one time usually matters
items.2: Your body turns carbohydrate into sugar, which raises your blood sugar. Both the kind and the amount matter
items.3: Carbohydrate is in grains and starches, fruit, some vegetables, legumes, milk and milk alternatives, sweet foods and many prepared foods. Meat and alternatives, most vegetables and fats have little
items.4: Diabetes Canada’s sheet gives about 45 to 60 g of carbohydrate at a meal and 15 to 30 g at a snack for most people. A dietitian or diabetes educator can help you set your own goals
items.5: Try to keep each meal and snack within 5 g of your goal
items.6: On a Nutrition Facts table, check the serving size first. Then take the total carbohydrate and subtract the fibre: 36 g of carbohydrate with 6 g of fibre counts as 30 g

2.note: If you take insulin with meals, work out with your team how carbohydrate and insulin fit together. This card covers counting only.

fields.5: Set with (my dietitian or diabetes educator)

3.title: Moving your body

items.1: Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of activity that raises your breathing and heart rate, like brisk walking, cycling, swimming or dancing
items.2: Spread it over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 days in a row off
items.3: Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes a day, and build up. Less than 150 minutes still has benefits
items.4: Add strength exercises at least 2 times a week, with weights, bands or your own body weight. If you’re new to them, get some instruction first
items.5: Break up long periods of sitting. Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests getting up briefly every 20 to 30 minutes
items.6: If you’ve been inactive for a while, talk to your doctor before starting anything harder than a brisk walk. If you have chest pain, pressure or discomfort, or you’re much more short of breath than usual, stop the activity and call 911 right away. These can be signs of a heart attack. Tell your doctor about it too, before you exercise again
items.7: Exercise can lower your blood sugar for up to 48 hours. If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, check regularly and carry fast-acting sugar. More in Staying Safe, under <link>Lows that sneak up</link>

3.note: Ask your team how to plan food and medicines around activity, especially if you use insulin.

4.title: Alcohol and cannabis

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s 2023 guideline says that if you don’t drink, it’s healthier not to start. If you do drink, talk with your team about what’s right for you
items.2: Diabetes Canada’s alcohol sheet says not to drink if you’re pregnant or trying to get pregnant, breastfeeding, have a personal or family history of drinking problems, are about to drive or do anything that needs your full attention, or take certain medicines. Ask your pharmacist about yours. The sheet is from 2018, so the drink limits printed on it are older than the 2023 advice on this card
items.3: If you take insulin or some other diabetes medicines, a low can come up to 24 hours after drinking. Eat carbohydrate when you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and make sure someone with you knows how to help, including calling 911 if you pass out. More in Staying Safe, under <link>Lows that sneak up</link>
items.4: Alternating alcoholic drinks with water helps you avoid getting dehydrated
items.5: Diabetes Canada’s 2023 guideline says that if you drink, cutting down lowers the risk to your health, and that this may mean no more than 2 standard drinks a week. Canada’s 2023 Guidance on Alcohol and Health says that at 2 standard drinks or fewer a week you’re likely to avoid harm from alcohol, that more than 2 at one time raises the risk of harms such as injuries, and that less is better. Your team can help if you want to cut down
items.6: Diabetes Canada does not recommend recreational cannabis for teens or adults with diabetes. With type 1, it says to avoid it, because it raises the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
items.7: If you do use cannabis, edibles can contain carbohydrate, and cannabis can make you hungrier. Diabetes Canada says adults who use it should be offered advice on lowering the risks

4.note: Alcohol and cannabis aren’t things to hide from your team. Diabetes Canada asks health-care providers to talk about them regularly, without judgement.

5.title: Distress, stress and sleep

items.1: Living with diabetes can feel like a burden. Diabetes Canada says its constant demands can lead to diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety
items.2: You may feel angry, guilty, frightened, discouraged or low. Diabetes Canada’s guideline calls these valid responses to a long-term condition
items.3: Depression is more common in people with diabetes, and there are effective treatments
items.4: Problems with eating, sleeping and stress are common too. Tell your team about them
items.5: So is fear of lows. If it’s holding you back, tell your team, because there are ways to help
items.6: Diabetes Canada’s guideline says everyone with diabetes, and parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes, should be checked regularly for diabetes distress. Your team may give you a short questionnaire to fill in before a visit
items.7: Regular activity can lower stress and help you relax and sleep

5.note: If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day, tell your diabetes team or your doctor rather than waiting it out.

figure.body: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.

6.title: Flying with diabetes supplies

items.1: Keep insulin and your supplies in your carry-on. Diabetes Canada says not to put insulin in checked luggage, because temperature changes can damage it
items.2: Insulin, and juice or gel to treat a low, can go through security in amounts over 100 mL. Declare them to the screening officer separately
items.3: Syringes are allowed with the needle guard on, as long as you’re carrying the medicine they’re for
items.4: Pumps and sensors are allowed. Diabetes Canada says not to wear them through the body scanner or put a pump through the X-ray machine. You can ask for a physical search instead, in private if you like
items.5: You don’t have to tell screening staff you have diabetes, and you don’t have to take off your pump. Just tell the screening officer you’re wearing one
items.6: CATSA suggests keeping medicine in its labelled packaging. Diabetes Canada suggests a letter from your doctor and a list of your medicines from your pharmacist
items.7: Pack spare insulin and supplies. In the heat, keep insulin in an insulated bag. In the cold, keep it close to your body so it doesn’t freeze

6.note: Crossing time zones can change when you take insulin or diabetes pills. Plan it with your doctor or diabetes educator before you go.

7.title: Driving

items.1: These steps are for people who take insulin, or a diabetes pill that can cause lows
items.2: Diabetes Canada suggests checking your blood sugar right before you drive, any time you feel low, and at least every 4 hours while driving, or wearing a real-time sensor
items.3: Don’t start driving if your blood sugar is below 4.0 mmol/L
items.4: After treating a low, wait at least 40 minutes, and until your blood sugar is at least 5.0 mmol/L, before you drive
items.5: If a low starts while you’re driving, stop somewhere safe, take the keys out of the ignition and treat it. The 40-minute wait applies here too
items.6: Keep fast-acting sugar within reach of the driver’s seat, and your meter and supplies with you
items.7: If you no longer feel the early signs of a low, or you’ve had a severe low in the past year, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says to check right before you drive and at least every 2 hours while driving, or wear a real-time sensor
items.8: A severe low is one where you pass out or need someone else’s help. If you have one while driving, the guideline says to stop driving right away. Tell your health-care provider and your driver licensing office right away, and do the same if you have more than one severe low while awake in the past 6 months (12 months for commercial drivers). Your provider may tell you not to drive
items.9: You have the right to be assessed for a driver’s licence as an individual. Licensing is handled by each province and territory. Licensing offices require a higher level of medical fitness to drive a bus, a commercial van, a transport truck or an emergency vehicle. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says commercial drivers should have a medical exam when they apply for their licence

7.note: Diabetes Canada uses 3.9 for a low in most of its guidance, and 4.0 for driving. This card uses 4.0 because the driving guideline does. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.

3.heading: If lows are harder to spot

8.title: Your feet, every day

items.1: Diabetes can damage the nerves and blood flow in your feet, so you may not feel a blister or cut, and it can be slower to heal
items.2: Wash your feet in warm, not hot, water and dry them well, especially between the toes
items.3: Check your feet and between your toes for cuts, blisters or changes. Use a hand mirror for the soles, or ask someone to help
items.4: Put lotion on your heels and soles, but not between your toes. Trim your nails straight across, not too short
items.5: Wear clean socks and well-fitting shoes. Test bath water with your hand before you step in
items.6: Have your bare feet checked by your doctor or a foot-care specialist, such as a podiatrist, chiropodist or foot-care nurse. Ask them to check for nerve damage and blood flow too
items.7: See your doctor or a foot-care specialist right away for swelling, warmth, redness or pain in your feet or legs, or for corns, calluses, ingrown toenails, warts or slivers. Don’t treat these yourself. An open sore (a foot ulcer) or signs of infection need care right away, even if they don’t hurt. Don’t wait if a sore gets more painful, red, warm, smelly or starts to drain, if your foot is red, warm and changing shape, or if skin turns black or your legs or feet hurt at rest: see your doctor right away or go to the emergency department. A serious foot infection doesn’t always cause a fever
items.8: Don’t go barefoot, even indoors. Don’t use over-the-counter corn or wart treatments, or put hot water bottles or heating pads on your feet

8.note: If you’ve been told your feet are at high risk, you may need checks more often, and shoes fitted by a professional.

9.title: Your eyes

items.1: Diabetes can damage the small blood vessels in the retina, at the back of the eye. This is called diabetic retinopathy
items.2: It often goes unnoticed until it affects your sight, so regular exams matter even when you see well
items.3: An optometrist or ophthalmologist does the exam, often after drops that widen your pupils
items.4: Diabetes Canada says to have an eye exam once a year, unless your optometrist or ophthalmologist suggests something different. With type 2, the first exam is at diagnosis. With type 1, yearly exams start 5 years after diagnosis, from age 15. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team
items.5: The Canadian Ophthalmological Society also suggests an exam at least once a year. If you’re planning a pregnancy, Diabetes Canada says to have an exam before you get pregnant and while you’re pregnant, and the Society suggests one in the first trimester
items.6: See an eye doctor right away if you notice dark spots, blurred, distorted or double vision, or large floaters. If you suddenly see flashes of light with a lot of new floaters, or part of your vision goes dark, don’t wait: see an eye doctor right away, or go to the emergency department if you can’t be seen today. It can be a sign of a torn or detached retina
items.7: Found early, retinopathy can often be treated successfully, and treatment can keep your sight from getting worse. Sight that has already been lost can’t be restored, which is why early exams matter
items.8: Keeping your blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range helps protect your eyes

9.note: If an exam finds little or no damage, Diabetes Canada’s guideline allows 1 to 2 years between exams with type 2. Your eye-care professional and diabetes team decide your schedule, and can share your results with each other.

10.title: Your kidneys

items.1: Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease in Canada. Up to half of people with diabetes will have signs of kidney damage in their lifetime
items.2: Good diabetes management and regular screening can prevent or delay the loss of kidney function
items.3: Most people have no symptoms early on, so screening is how kidney disease is found
items.4: Screening is two tests: a urine test (ACR) that looks for protein, and a blood test (eGFR) that shows how well your kidneys are working
items.5: With type 2, screening starts at diagnosis. With type 1, it starts 5 years after diagnosis. After that, it’s once a year
items.6: Keeping your blood sugar and blood pressure at target, not smoking, and taking your medicines as prescribed all help protect your kidneys
items.7: If you have kidney disease, a dietitian can tell you whether to change how much protein, potassium, phosphate or salt you eat
items.8: Diabetes Canada’s 2025 kidney guideline says some diabetes medicines also help protect the kidneys and heart. Ask your team whether yours does, and don’t change a medicine on your own

10.note: Ask your team for your ACR and eGFR results, and what they mean for you. Children follow their own schedule, so ask your child’s team.

11.title: Your heart: the ABCDEs

items.1: Diabetes raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. Heart disease may come 15 years earlier than in people without diabetes
items.2: You can lower that risk considerably by working on all your risk factors with your team. Diabetes Canada sums them up as the ABCDEs
items.3: A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over time. Most people aim for 7% or less
items.4: Most people aim for a blood pressure below 130/80
items.5: The usual LDL (“bad”) cholesterol target is below 2.0 mmol/L
items.6: Some medicines protect the heart. Ask your team whether any are right for you
items.7: Regular physical activity and healthy eating
items.8: Screening for complications in your heart, feet, kidneys and eyes; stopping smoking, with help if you want it; and self-management, including handling stress
items.9: Diabetes Canada suggests having your blood pressure checked at every diabetes visit, your A1C every 3 months, and your cholesterol every year, or more often if you take medicine to lower it

11.note: Your targets are yours to set with your team. Diabetes Canada notes that A1C targets are different in pregnancy, for older adults and for children 12 and under.

4.heading: D · Drugs to protect your heart

12.title: Work and your rights

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s position is that people with diabetes should be eligible for any job they’re qualified for
items.2: It also says people should have the right to look after their diabetes in public places
items.3: It says people with diabetes have the right to care that supports the best quality of life wherever they are, including in hospital and long-term care
items.4: For a driver’s licence, you have the right to be assessed as an individual. More in <link>Driving</link>
items.5: Coverage for medicines, supplies and devices varies across Canada, and you may be eligible for the Disability Tax Credit
items.6: Diabetes Canada’s information and support line is 1-800-226-8464

12.note: Diabetes Canada publishes position statements on employment, insurance and self-care in public places. They’re linked from its rights pages.

1.heading: Eyes
1.body: Once a year, unless your eye-care professional suggests something different. Type 2: the first exam at diagnosis. Type 1: from age 15, starting 5 years after diagnosis. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team. See Your eyes.

2.heading: Kidneys
2.body: A urine test (ACR) and a blood test (eGFR) once a year: from diagnosis with type 2, and from 5 years after diagnosis with type 1. See Your kidneys.

3.heading: Feet
3.body: A bare-foot check by your doctor or a foot-care specialist at least once a year, including nerves and blood flow, and more often if you’re at high risk. In between, check them yourself every day: see Your feet, every day.

4.heading: Heart
4.body: Blood pressure at every diabetes visit, A1C about every 3 months or as your team advises, and cholesterol once a year. See Your heart: the ABCDEs.

1.title: 9-8-8: call or text, any time
1.body: If you are thinking about suicide, or worried about someone who is. Free, 24/7, in English and French. If your safety is at risk, call 911.

2.body: Diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety, and when to reach out to your health-care team.

3.body: Planning a trip, and buying travel insurance.

1.body: At work, in public, and in hospital and long-term care.

2.body: For discrimination by a federally regulated employer or service. The Commission also helps you work out where to go instead, such as your province’s or territory’s human rights commission.

1.body: Free live online sessions led by registered health professionals, for people newly diagnosed or wanting a refresher.

2.title: InfoDiabetes Service
2.body: Questions about diabetes, answered by Diabetes Québec’s health professionals by phone, email or chat. Not an emergency service: for an emergency, call 911.

pharmacist.body: The Certified Diabetes Educators at Bayshore Express Pharmacy, the Liivv pharmacy in Markham, Ontario, answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to the Liivv pharmacy in your province. Your targets, your medicines and your checkups belong with your diabetes team.

closing.body: Most of this becomes routine: a look at your feet, some movement most days, a few checkups a year. The rest is knowing who to ask.

know-your-type.title: Know Your Type
know-your-type.heroBody: The common types of diabetes, the less common ones, and the clues that your type might be different. Your team decides your type. This chapter helps you ask.
know-your-type.focus: The common types: type 1 at any age, type 2, prediabetes, gestational diabetes, and how type 1 starts before symptoms. Less common types: when your type might be different, LADA, MODY, diabetes in babies, genetic syndromes, pancreas conditions and iron overload, cystic fibrosis-related diabetes, and diabetes from medicines or after a transplant.
know-your-type.vibe: Clear and curious: what each type is, and the right questions to ask.

categoriesIntro.heading: What your type means
categoriesIntro.body: Most people have one of the common types. Some have a less common type, and for some the type becomes clearer over time. This chapter explains each one, and the clues worth raising with your team. Your team decides your type.

startHere.heading: One of the common types, or something less common?

1.title: Type 1, including in adults

items.1: Diabetes Canada says 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1. In type 1, the pancreas makes no insulin, so insulin is taken by injection or with a pump
items.2: Type 1 can start in adulthood. Breakthrough T1D estimates that about 71% of people with type 1 in Canada were diagnosed as adults
items.3: Breakthrough T1D also says 85% have no family connection to type 1
items.4: Signs your team looks for include type 1 antibodies in the blood, very little insulin of your own (a low C-peptide), and a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
items.5: Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline names automated insulin delivery as the preferred option for anyone willing and able to use it. Otherwise, it recommends a sensor (CGM) with a pump or with injections

1.note: <link>Ketones and DKA</link> are covered in Staying Safe. The test names are explained in Could my type be different?

2.title: Type 2

items.1: Type 2 is the most common type. Diabetes Canada says 90 to 95% of people with diabetes have it
items.2: Risk factors include being over 40, having diabetes in your family, and your ethnic background. Type 2 may cause no symptoms
items.3: Diabetes Canada diagnoses diabetes with any one of these results:
items.4: A fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L or higher
items.5: An A1C of 6.5% or higher, in adults. It isn’t used when type 1 is suspected
items.6: A blood sugar of 11.1 mmol/L or higher, 2 hours after a glucose drink or at any time of day
items.7: Without symptoms, a second test on another day confirms it
items.8: With symptoms of high blood sugar, Diabetes Canada says the diagnosis is made without a second test, and treatment shouldn’t be delayed. Contact your doctor or another health-care provider today, without waiting for a second test. <link>Emergency signs</link> are in Staying Safe
items.9: For children and teens with type 2, Diabetes Canada says antibody testing should be considered, because up to 10 to 20% test positive

2.note: If your diabetes doesn’t fit the usual picture, see Could my type be different?

3.title: Prediabetes

items.1: Prediabetes means a blood sugar above the usual range, but below the numbers for diabetes. Diabetes Canada uses any one of these results:
items.2: A fasting blood sugar of 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L
items.3: An A1C of 6.0 to 6.4%
items.4: A blood sugar of 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L, 2 hours after a glucose drink
items.5: Diabetes Canada’s Prediabetes page links to the CANRISK test
items.6: Not everyone with prediabetes goes on to develop type 2, but Diabetes Canada says many people do

3.note: Ask your doctor what your numbers mean for you, and when to test again.

4.title: Gestational, or diabetes from before pregnancy?

items.1: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found during pregnancy. Diabetes from before pregnancy, type 1 or type 2, was diagnosed before you conceived
items.2: Diabetes that is clearly there early in pregnancy is counted on its own, as overt diabetes, not as gestational diabetes
items.3: If you’re at high risk, Diabetes Canada’s guideline includes an A1C test before 20 weeks
items.4: Screening for gestational diabetes is offered between 24 and 28 weeks
items.5: Diabetes Canada says gestational diabetes affects 3 to 20% of pregnancies and usually goes away after birth. It raises the chance of type 2 and heart disease later
items.6: After the birth, Diabetes Canada recommends a glucose tolerance test between 6 weeks and 6 months
items.7: International guidance from the University of Exeter says a steady fasting blood sugar of 5.5 to 8 mmol/L, with diabetes in the family, can point to a single-gene type called GCK-MODY. If that sounds like you, tell your team early in pregnancy

4.note: Fill in the reminder with your team before the birth. Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 is covered in This Might Be You.

fields.2: My glucose tolerance test, between 6 weeks and 6 months after the birth, is booked for
fields.3: Who orders it, and where I go

5.title: Type 1 starts before symptoms

items.1: Type 1 starts before there are symptoms. Breakthrough T1D describes stages 1 and 2 coming before diagnosis, and international guidance defines the stages like this:
items.2: Stage 1: two or more type 1 antibodies, with normal blood sugar
items.3: Stage 2: two or more type 1 antibodies, with blood sugar starting to rise above normal
items.4: Stage 3: type 1 diabetes is diagnosed
items.5: Breakthrough T1D says two or more antibodies that last over time mean a high risk of type 1. Only 10 to 15% of people newly diagnosed have a family history
items.6: TrialNet screens relatives of people with type 1 at no cost, with a home finger-stick kit or a lab visit, anywhere in Canada. Immediate relatives aged 2 to 45 and other relatives aged 2 to 20 can take part. Results take 4 to 6 weeks
items.7: Breakthrough T1D also lists FEDERATE-Can, in Quebec. CanScreen, a Canadian research program on screening newborns and children, says it is launching in fall 2026 or winter 2027
items.8: Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline makes no recommendation about screening
items.9: People who test positive are followed over time. International guidance says they should be taught, and reminded, about the signs of diabetes and DKA
items.10: In May 2025, Health Canada approved teplizumab (Tzield) for people aged 8 and older in stage 2, to delay stage 3. Canada’s Drug Agency says that in one study it delayed stage 3 by about 2 years, and that it can cause side effects, including serious ones. The agency recommended that public drug plans not cover it, and Diabetes Canada says it isn’t on any provincial or territorial drug plan. It’s available out of pocket, through private insurance, or through compassionate access
items.11: Breakthrough T1D also says you can ask your doctor to look at UncoverT1D, a website run by Sanofi, the company that makes teplizumab, that has information for health care providers about which tests to order

5.note: Whether to screen, and what a result means, is a conversation with your doctor. A screening result isn’t a diagnosis.

6.title: Could my type be different?

items.1: Your diabetes team decides your type. Diabetes Canada says some cases are difficult to classify
items.2: An international consensus from the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes found that more than 40% of people who develop type 1 after age 30 are first treated as type 2
items.3: Diabetes Canada says the right type may change your treatment. International guidance adds that it can show whether your family might be offered testing

2.heading: Clues to mention to your team

items.1: You were diagnosed at a younger age, or you have a lower body weight
items.2: You lost weight without trying, or you’ve had ketones or DKA
items.3: You needed insulin within 1 to 2 years of diagnosis
items.4: Diabetes runs through generations of your family, such as a parent and a grandparent
items.5: You were diagnosed before 6 months of age
items.6: You have hearing loss, and there’s diabetes on your mother’s side of the family. International guidance links the two
items.7: You’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, or you have cystic fibrosis or iron overload (hemochromatosis)
items.8: Your diabetes started after a transplant, or after you began steroids, an antipsychotic, an anti-rejection medicine or cancer immunotherapy
items.9: You have a hormone condition, such as Cushing’s syndrome or acromegaly

items.1: Antibody tests look for signs of type 1. International guidance suggests testing for GAD antibodies first
items.2: A C-peptide test shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s most useful months to years after diagnosis, and not during a very high blood sugar
items.3: Genetic tests look for single-gene types, such as MODY. A specialist usually arranges them
items.4: Diabetes Canada says antibody levels fade over time, and the tests aren’t accurate enough to use for everyone. When your type is hard to tell, a positive test points to type 1, but a negative test doesn’t rule type 1 out. Your team decides

items.1: Your doctor or specialist orders these tests. In Manitoba, for example, the GAD antibody test is ordered by endocrinologists, and other doctors need an approval form
items.2: What’s covered varies by province. In BC, for example, the antibody tests aren’t covered by MSP
items.3: Genetic testing usually needs a referral. A test that isn’t offered in your province may need approval before it’s sent elsewhere

6.note: Not a diagnostic tool. These clues are things to mention, not signs that your type is wrong. Your team decides what to test. Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist.

figure.printHeading: Questions to bring to your team

questions.1: Does my type still fit, given the clues I’ve ticked?
questions.2: Have I had antibody tests? What did they show?
questions.3: Would a C-peptide test help, and when?
questions.4: Should anyone in my family be tested?
questions.5: Would a specialist or a genetics clinic help?

figure.glossaryNote: Where Canadian guidance doesn’t explain a test, the meaning here comes from international guidance.

1.meaning: The antibody test most often done first when type 1 or LADA is possible.

2.meaning: Other type 1 antibodies, also used in screening. IA-2 and ZnT8 may be tested if the GAD test is negative.

3.meaning: Shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s a blood or urine test.

4.meaning: A blood test that reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. Diabetes Canada uses it to diagnose diabetes and prediabetes. With diabetes, it’s usually checked about every 3 months.

5.meaning: Your blood sugar is checked 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink.

6.meaning: A genetic test that looks at many diabetes genes at once.

7.title: LADA: type 1 that starts slowly in adults

items.1: LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) is a slow-starting form of type 1. It’s sometimes called type 1.5
items.2: The usual pattern: it starts after age 30, antibodies are present, and insulin isn’t needed for at least the first 6 months
items.3: It’s often first diagnosed and managed as type 2
items.4: An antibody test, usually GAD, confirms it. International guidance says a C-peptide test helps guide treatment
items.5: Most people need insulin sooner than with type 2, and the timing varies widely. International guidance says it tends to come sooner with higher antibody levels, or more than one antibody
items.6: Breakthrough T1D describes a modified type 1 plan, which can include some type 2 medicines. International guidance says others are less suitable, so ask your team before any change
items.7: Estimates of how common it is range from 2 to 12% of adult diabetes (an international consensus) to about 10% (Breakthrough T1D)

7.note: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Bring these questions to your team. The signs of lows and ketones are in Staying Safe.

figure.heading: LADA: questions to bring to your team

fields.1: Have I had an antibody test? What did it show?
fields.3: When should I check for ketones, and how?

8.title: MODY: single-gene diabetes

items.1: MODY is caused by a change in a single gene. Diabetes Canada calls single-gene diabetes rare. International estimates range from 1 to 2% of diabetes for MODY (Diabetes UK, University of Exeter) to 1 to 5% for all single-gene types (the US NIDDK)
items.2: Diabetes UK says about 9 in 10 people with MODY are first told they have another type
items.3: Clues include being diagnosed young, not having obesity, having no type 1 antibodies, and a parent with diabetes, in two or more generations
items.4: How young varies. Diabetes Canada and Diabetes UK use under 25. Other international guidance uses under 30, or 35 and under. Your team decides
items.5: It’s confirmed with a genetic test, usually after antibody and C-peptide tests
items.6: GCK: a mild, steady high blood sugar that usually needs no treatment
items.7: HNF1A and HNF4A: often treated with tablets rather than insulin. A specialist decides
items.8: HNF1B: can affect the kidneys, with cysts, and other organs. It’s usually treated with insulin
items.9: Each child of a parent with MODY has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Once the family’s gene change is known, relatives can be tested, and genetic counselling can help
items.10: In pregnancy with GCK, care depends on whether the baby inherited it, so tell your team early. HNF4A can mean a larger baby, and low blood sugar in the newborn
items.11: In a Canadian study of children with single-gene diabetes, GCK was the most common type: 19 of 29 children
items.12: Most of the evidence comes from people of European ancestry. The usual clues are less reliable for people of other ancestries

8.note: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Fill in the family tree before your appointment. It helps your team, or a genetic counsellor, see the pattern.

familyTree.heading: My family diabetes tree
familyTree.intro: For your appointment. Fill in what you know and leave the rest blank. It doesn’t work out a risk, and nothing you type is saved or sent.

sides.yours: Me, my brothers and sisters, and my children

9.title: Diabetes in babies

items.1: Diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age is usually caused by a single gene
items.2: Diabetes Canada says every baby diagnosed before 6 months should have genetic testing
items.3: The University of Exeter says it affects about 1 in 100,000 births. The US NIDDK says about 1 in 90,000, and describes it in the first 6 to 12 months
items.4: Some forms are temporary, and others are lifelong
items.5: The genetic result matters. For the potassium-channel types, international guidance says about 9 in 10 people can switch from insulin to tablets under specialist care, with more benefit the earlier it happens
items.6: Adults told they have type 1 who were diagnosed before 6 months should have their diagnosis reviewed

9.note: Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change in treatment is planned with a specialist team.

10.title: Genetic syndromes with diabetes

items.1: Some single-gene types come with other health signs, such as hearing loss or vision loss
items.2: MIDD (maternally inherited diabetes and deafness) passes from a mother to all her children, though how much it affects each child varies. Fathers don’t pass it on
items.3: Diabetes starts at 37 on average, and insulin is usually needed within about 2 years
items.4: Hearing loss is common and often comes first. The heart, kidneys, eyes and gut can be affected too
items.5: A urine sample is preferred for the test
items.6: Wolfram syndrome is very rare, about 1 in 500,000 people, and both parents carry the gene. Diabetes usually starts around age 6, and vision loss from the optic nerve around age 11
items.7: Lipodystrophy affects where the body stores fat. Clues include little or unusually placed body fat, high triglycerides (a blood fat), and darkened skin in body folds
items.8: These are confirmed with genetic testing, arranged through a specialist

10.note: If several of these sound familiar, ask your team whether a genetics referral would help.

11.title: Pancreas conditions and iron overload

items.1: Diabetes Canada lists diseases of the pancreas as a cause of diabetes, including pancreatitis, surgery or injury to the pancreas, a growth in the pancreas, and cystic fibrosis
items.2: Hemochromatosis, where the body stores too much iron, is on the same list. The Canadian Hemochromatosis Society says it can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes
items.3: About 1 in 300 Canadians have two copies of the gene change that puts them at risk. BC’s guideline says fewer than 1 in 10 of them develop the disease
items.4: An iron test isn’t part of a standard blood test, so it has to be asked for. A genetic test confirms hemochromatosis
items.5: Close family, such as parents, brothers, sisters and children, should be tested
items.6: Treatment removes blood regularly (phlebotomy). The society says it can mildly improve diabetes

11.note: If you’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, ask your team what it means for your diabetes care. Lows and ketones are covered in Staying Safe.

12.title: Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes

items.1: Cystic fibrosis can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes, called cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD)
items.2: It becomes more common with age. In Canada, 3.6% of people with CF under 18 have it, rising to 58.7% of adults over 35
items.3: Screening is yearly from age 10, through your CF clinic. Cystic Fibrosis Canada’s guideline starts with an A1C test and adds a glucose tolerance test when needed. The glucose tolerance test may be used first if A1C isn’t reliable for you. Your clinic decides
items.4: Insulin is the main treatment, and the only medicine used for children. Cystic Fibrosis Canada says some adults may have other options
items.5: If you use insulin, ask your team for a plan for lows. Cystic Fibrosis Canada’s guideline says people on insulin, and their families or carers, should be taught how to use glucagon. International guidance adds that the body’s own response to a low is weaker in CF
items.6: In pregnancy, if you don’t already have CFRD, a glucose tolerance test is done early, at 12 to 16 weeks or when the pregnancy is confirmed. If that one is normal, it’s repeated at 24 to 28 weeks
items.7: After a transplant, 25 to 50% of people with CF who didn’t have CFRD before develop diabetes
items.8: Yearly eye, kidney and nerve checks start 5 years after diagnosis
items.9: Your CF clinic works with a diabetes team, ideally including a diabetes educator

12.note: Glucagon and <link>the Rule of 15</link> are in Staying Safe.

13.title: From medicines, or after a transplant

items.1: Diabetes Canada lists some medicines that can cause diabetes, including steroids, some antipsychotics and some anti-rejection medicines
items.2: Diabetes Canada’s hospital guideline says 20 to 50% of people without diabetes who take steroids develop high blood sugar. Checking blood sugar for 48 hours after starting may be considered
items.3: Some antipsychotic medicines can cause weight gain and raise blood sugar and cholesterol
items.4: In children and teens, the risk of type 2 diabetes is 2 to 3 times higher, and the rise can show within the first year
items.5: Diabetes Canada recommends checking weight, blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol before you start, then on a schedule that differs for each check. Ask your prescriber when yours are due
items.6: International guidance from the American Diabetes Association says to check blood sugar before you start a checkpoint inhibitor, a type of cancer immunotherapy, and at every visit while you’re on it. An international consensus says this diabetes can come on with DKA
items.7: After a transplant, the risk depends on things like the steroid dose, some infections, and which anti-rejection medicine is used
items.8: Diabetes Canada’s guideline checks blood sugar before the transplant, in the first 3 months after it, and with an A1C at 3 and 12 months, then every year. It says a glucose tolerance test is more sensitive than A1C, and it’s used if A1C isn’t reliable. Your team decides
items.9: An international consensus says 20 to 40% of people who have a heart, lung or liver transplant develop diabetes
items.10: Know the <link>signs of high blood sugar and ketones</link>. They’re in Staying Safe

13.note: Don’t stop or change how you take any of these medicines on your own, even if your blood sugar goes up. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist first.

1.heading: Your doctor or specialist
1.body: Orders antibody, C-peptide and A1C tests. Some labs limit antibody tests to specialists unless an approval form is sent. Bring your clues: see Could my type be different?

2.heading: A genetics clinic
2.body: Single-gene testing usually needs a referral. A test not offered in your province may need approval first. See MODY: single-gene diabetes.

3.heading: TrialNet, for relatives
3.body: Free type 1 antibody screening for relatives, at home or at a lab, anywhere in Canada. See Type 1 starts before symptoms.

4.heading: Your CF clinic
4.body: Yearly diabetes screening from age 10 for people with cystic fibrosis. See Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.

pharmacist.heading: Questions about pumps, sensors, supplies or claims
pharmacist.body: The Certified Diabetes Educators at Bayshore Express Pharmacy, the Liivv pharmacy in Markham, Ontario, answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to the Liivv pharmacy in your province. Questions about your type, and the tests for it, belong with your diabetes team.

closing.heading: Knowing your type
closing.body: Your type shapes your care, and it can be looked at again if something doesn’t fit. Bring your clues and your questions to your team.
