categoriesIntro.heading: When the usual advice isn’t enough
categoriesIntro.body: Most diabetes information is written for an adult managing on their own. These are the times when the details change, and the best next step is usually a conversation with a particular person.

startHere.heading: A season of life, or someone you care for?

1.title: Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s guideline recommends planning a pregnancy with your diabetes team before you start trying
items.2: Its A1C target before conception is 7.0% or lower, and 6.5% or lower if it can be done safely. Your team sets yours
items.3: It recommends starting folic acid before you conceive. With diabetes, you may need a higher dose than is usually advised, so ask your team or pharmacist how much to take
items.4: Bring a list of all your medicines, so your team can review them before you try. Some medicines need to be stopped or changed before pregnancy. Don’t stop any on your own
items.5: The guideline recommends an eye exam and a kidney check before you conceive

items.1: Blood sugar targets are tighter in pregnancy. Your team will give you yours
items.2: With type 1, Diabetes Canada’s guideline recommends a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) in pregnancy. With type 2, ask your team whether one suits you
items.3: The guideline recommends another eye exam in the first trimester
items.4: In pregnancy, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) can happen even when blood sugar is normal or only a little high. DKA needs medical care right away

items.1: If you use insulin, your needs drop quickly after the birth. Plan the change with your team before you deliver. Lows are more likely in the first days, so check more often
items.2: The guideline encourages breastfeeding
items.3: It also recommends an eye exam within the first year after the birth

1.note: Gestational diabetes, which starts in pregnancy, is in <link>Know Your Type</link>. This card draws mostly on Diabetes Canada’s pregnancy guideline for health professionals and its key messages for people planning a pregnancy. That guideline is from 2018, and Diabetes Canada is updating it.

fields.2: Folic acid: how much, and when to start
fields.3: My medicines: what stays the same, and what changes
fields.4: Eye and kidney checks booked for
fields.5: Who to call while I’m pregnant

2.title: A child with type 1

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline sets the same A1C target for children of every age: below 7.0%. Your child’s team sets theirs
items.2: Younger children take less fast-acting sugar for a low, depending on their age. The amounts are in <link>The Rule of 15</link>
items.3: From age 4, glucagon can be a nasal spray or an injection. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep
items.4: Check for ketones when your child is sick or their blood sugar stays high. The ranges are in <link>Ketones: check and act</link>
items.5: The guideline says regular check-ins on emotional health are especially helpful in the teen years and young adulthood
items.6: Type 1 diabetes meets the Disability Tax Credit’s life-sustaining therapy test for 2021 and later tax years. You still apply with form T2201, on paper or online, and your child’s doctor or nurse practitioner fills in their part
items.7: Once a child is approved for the credit, a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) can be opened for them
items.8: Some provincial pump programs have separate rules for children. In Quebec, a child has to join the pump program before age 18
items.9: Kidney checks usually start 5 years after diagnosis, or after puberty if your child was diagnosed young. Eye exams usually start at age 15, once your child has had type 1 for 5 years. Your child’s team sets the schedule

2.note: Your child’s diabetes clinic is the first call for anything about their plan. Programs by province are in <link>Funding & Coverage</link>.

3.title: Your child at school

items.1: Diabetes Canada says a student’s care plan has two parts: a daily diabetes management plan and a diabetes emergency plan
items.2: Diabetes Canada says the principal should work with you, your child and your child’s health care team to write the plan
items.3: The Canadian Paediatric Society recommends talking it through before the school year starts, and having at least two staff trained
items.4: Diabetes Canada says students should be able to check their blood sugar, take insulin, and treat lows and highs wherever and whenever they need to
items.5: Diabetes Canada says schools should let students carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar
items.6: Diabetes@School says lows at school are common for students with type 1. They’re no cause for alarm, but they need treating right away, where they happen
items.7: Don’t leave a student alone if a low is suspected. If they’re unresponsive, have a seizure or can’t take sugar by mouth, it’s an emergency: have someone call 911, turn them on their side, stay with them, and put nothing in their mouth
items.8: Then, if the care plan includes consent for glucagon, staff named in the plan, and trained, give it
items.9: Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline calls for help with giving insulin at school and daycare across Canada

3.note: School rules differ by province and territory, and Diabetes Canada compares them. Diabetes@School, from the Canadian Paediatric Society and its partners, has more for families and school staff.

fields.1: Who at school is trained (at least two people)
fields.2: Where the low supplies are kept
fields.3: Glucagon: is it in the plan, and who gives it
fields.4: How my child checks their blood sugar at school
fields.5: Who the school calls first, and the backup number
fields.6: Who calls 911 for a severe low

4.title: Later life

items.1: Diabetes Canada’s guideline for older people sets targets by how healthy and independent someone is
items.2: For people who are healthy and independent, the A1C target is 7.0% or lower
items.3: For people who take medicine that can cause lows, the guideline says a less strict A1C target may be considered: 7.1 to 8.0% for people who are functionally dependent, and 7.1 to 8.5% for people who are frail or living with dementia. Your team sets yours. Near the end of life, the guideline says A1C tests are no longer recommended. The aim then is to avoid any lows, and highs that cause symptoms
items.4: The guideline puts a strong focus on preventing lows in older people
items.5: If injecting is getting harder, ask your team about simpler options. The guideline names prefilled insulin pens as one way to cut down on dose mistakes
items.6: Changes in memory or thinking can make a new skill, like injecting, harder to learn. Tell your team, so they can plan around it
items.7: In Ontario, people 65 and older who use insulin every day and live at home can apply to the Assistive Devices Program for $170 a year toward syringes and needles

4.note: Ask a pharmacist to go through your full list of medicines, including anything you buy without a prescription. More programs for seniors are in <link>Funding & Coverage</link>. This card draws on Diabetes Canada’s guideline for health professionals and its key messages for older people.

5.title: Caring for someone with diabetes

items.1: The most useful things to learn are what a low and a high look like, <link>the Rule of 15</link>, and when to call for help. They’re all in Staying Safe
items.2: If they have glucagon, ask to be shown how it works. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says the people around them should be taught
items.3: Ask what kind of help is wanted before you offer it
items.4: Breakthrough T1D has a caregiver guide for parents and caregivers of children and teens with type 1
items.5: Its Mental Health + Diabetes Directory lists registered mental health providers, for people living with diabetes and the people affected by it
items.6: Low mood and worry about lows are common with diabetes, and Diabetes Canada’s guideline asks teams to check for them

5.note: If caring is wearing you down, tell your own doctor. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes should be checked for diabetes distress too.

figure.body: If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911.

6.title: First Nations and Inuit: NIHB coverage

items.1: Indigenous Services Canada runs the federal Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program for First Nations and Inuit
items.2: Who is eligible is set out on <link>Indigenous Services Canada’s eligibility page</link>. Liivv can’t decide whether you’re eligible. For questions about eligibility, Indigenous Services Canada says to contact your NIHB regional office
items.3: For people who manage diabetes with insulin, NIHB covers several continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), with prior approval. The list is in <link>the NIHB program updates</link>
items.4: It also covers up to 800 test strips every 100 days for people who use insulin
items.5: If you aren’t covered by NIHB, <link>Funding & Coverage</link> lists the programs in each province and territory

6.note: NIHB adds items to its list from time to time. Your pharmacist can check what’s covered today.

1.heading: Planning a pregnancy
1.body: Your diabetes team, before you start trying, to go over your A1C, your medicines, and your eyes and kidneys. More in Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2.

2.heading: A child starting school
2.body: The principal, with you, your child and their diabetes team, before the school year starts. More in Your child at school.

3.heading: Later life
3.body: Your diabetes team, for targets that fit your health, and a pharmacist, for your full list of medicines. More in Later life.

4.heading: Someone you care for
4.body: Staying Safe for the basics, and Breakthrough T1D’s caregiver guide if it’s a child or teen with type 1. More in Caring for someone with diabetes.

pharmacist.heading: Supply questions, whoever you’re shopping for
pharmacist.body: The Certified Diabetes Educators at Bayshore Express Pharmacy, the Liivv pharmacy in Markham, Ontario, answer questions from anywhere in Canada: pumps, sensors, meters, supplies, billing and claims. When needed, they pass you to the Liivv pharmacy in your province. Questions about a pregnancy, a child’s plan or a change in someone’s health belong with their diabetes team.

closing.heading: The same diabetes, a different season
closing.body: What changes is who to bring in, and when. Knowing that is most of the work.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical advice. Care in pregnancy, for children and in later life differs in ways this page doesn’t try to cover. It tells you what changes and who to ask. Your diabetes team sets your targets and your plan.

urgentExit.lead: Signs that need emergency care are in Staying Safe, under

type.other: Another type (such as LADA or type 3c), or not sure

therapy.nonInsulin: Tablets, or injections that aren’t insulin

fed-nihb.covered: NIHB continues to cover these glucose sensors (CGM) for clients who manage their diabetes with insulin: FreeStyle Libre 2, Dexcom G6 and G7, and Guardian Connect. FreeStyle Libre 3 with prior approval, at one reader every 3 years and 14 sensors every 6 months. Guardian 4, as a limited use benefit with prior approval, for people with type 1 aged 19 or under on intensive insulin who use a MiniMed 780G. If you use insulin, test strips up to 800 every 100 days.
fed-nihb.who: Who is eligible is set out on Indigenous Services Canada’s NIHB pages. Liivv can’t decide whether you’re eligible: ask NIHB or your pharmacy.
fed-nihb.howToApply: NIHB covers items on its Drug Benefit List when they aren’t covered by provincial or territorial health insurance, private insurance or another public plan. Pharmacies enrolled with NIHB generally bill it directly, so you don’t pay a deductible or co-payment: you show your client identification. Some items, such as some sensors, need prior approval first.

fed-vac.covered: A continuous glucose monitor for type 1 diabetes, under benefit code 401140, once every 5 calendar years, with a prescription from a doctor or nurse practitioner. A replacement device doesn’t need a new prescription.
fed-vac.who: If you’re a Veterans Affairs Canada client with type 1 diabetes, this benefit may cover you. Ask Veterans Affairs Canada whether it applies to you.
fed-vac.howToApply: It needs pre-authorization, so get that before you buy.
fed-vac.notes: Veterans Affairs Canada’s general medical supplies policy also names diabetic test strips, syringes and needles among its examples.

on-adp-pump.covered: 100% of the ADP price of an insulin pump. For pump supplies, up to $2,400 a year, paid to you as $600 every 3 months.
on-adp-pump.who: People with type 1 diabetes who meet the program’s medical criteria. It isn’t based on income. If WSIB or Veterans Affairs Canada already pays for the same items, ADP doesn’t.
on-adp-pump.howToApply: An ADP-registered diabetes education program assesses you, and an ADP-registered vendor sends in the application. ADP aims to review applications within 8 weeks, and the first $600 is sent within 30 days of approval. Renew pump supplies every year.
on-adp-pump.notes: After the 5-year warranty, a worn-out pump can be replaced; ADP asks for a repair quote. A replacement is also covered if your medical needs have changed. ADP doesn’t cover replacing a lost pump or supplies, or repairing ones damaged through misuse or neglect.

bc-pharmacare-pumps.covered: One insulin pump every 5 years: the Omnipod 5 or Omnipod DASH system, the mylife YpsoPump, or the MiniMed 670G, 770G or 780G. On Fair PharmaCare you pay until you reach your deductible, then PharmaCare pays 70%, and 100% once you reach your family maximum. On Plans B, C, F and W it pays 100%. Pump supplies (pods, infusion sets, reservoirs and cartridges) are covered whether or not PharmaCare paid for your pump, with no Special Authority needed; batteries and adhesive pads aren’t.
bc-pharmacare-pumps.who: People covered by Fair PharmaCare or Plan B, C, F or W, with type 1 or another form of diabetes that needs insulin, whose endocrinologist or diabetes specialist confirms they meet the medical criteria.
bc-pharmacare-pumps.howToApply: Your specialist sends PharmaCare a Special Authority request. If it’s approved, you get a copy of the approval letter to take to the pump maker; the approval lasts 6 months. Wait for the letter before you buy: PharmaCare can’t cover a pump bought before approval. Pump supplies are covered when a pharmacy or an approved pump vendor submits the claim on PharmaNet; PharmaCare doesn’t take paper claims for them.
bc-pharmacare-pumps.notes: No Tandem pump is on PharmaCare’s list of covered pumps. Tandem pump supplies, such as t:slim cartridges and AutoSoft, TruSteel and VariSoft infusion sets, are on its list of diabetes products.

ab-iptp.covered: An insulin pump every 5 years from an approved maker (Medtronic, Ypsomed, Insulet or Tandem), its supplies, and other diabetes management supplies, up to set limits.
ab-iptp.who: Alberta residents enrolled in, or eligible for, the Alberta Health Care Insurance Plan, with type 1 or type 3c diabetes, who meet the program’s clinical criteria. Adults have a review every year, and children under 18 every 6 months.
ab-iptp.howToApply: Through an approved insulin pump clinic: you attend a pre-pump information session, complete an education plan, have at least one assessment and sign a Patient Responsibility Form. The clinic then sends Alberta Blue Cross an eligibility form, and Alberta Blue Cross mails you a confirmation letter. Pumps come straight from an approved maker, and supplies from a licensed Alberta pharmacy or an approved maker, which bill the program directly. The program doesn’t pay you back for a pump or supplies you pay for yourself.
ab-iptp.notes: Since October 1, 2026, Alberta’s government programs, this one included, pay only after any private or workplace plan you have.

sk-pump.covered: A $6,300 grant toward one insulin pump every 5 years. Pump supplies follow your Drug Plan coverage, so deductibles and co-payments apply.
sk-pump.who: People with type 1 diabetes who would benefit from a pump and meet the program’s criteria.
sk-pump.howToApply: A Saskatchewan Health Authority diabetes education program, or an authorized diabetes specialist physician, sends in the application. For children, it goes through the Saskatchewan Health Authority’s pediatric diabetes education program, after an information session or an online module.

mb-pump.covered: One approved insulin pump every 5 years, ordered from an approved supplier at no cost to you, with no deductible. Pump supplies aren’t part of it: they can be covered by Manitoba Pharmacare, where your deductible applies.
mb-pump.who: Manitobans 18 and over with type 1 diabetes whom an endocrinologist, or the doctor who manages their diabetes, recommends for a pump. You can’t have had a pump from a Manitoba government program in the last 5 years, or have coverage under a federal program.
mb-pump.howToApply: Your endocrinologist or doctor sends the application to Manitoba Health for you. If it’s approved, you get a letter telling you how to order your pump directly from the supplier.
mb-pump.notes: Children have a separate program, the Manitoba Pediatric Insulin Pump Program (MPIPP). Ask your child’s diabetes team about it.

qc-pump.covered: Up to $6,300 toward a pump every 5 years, and up to $4,000 a year for pump supplies.
qc-pump.who: You have to join before you turn 18. You can stay in after 18, with a review each year. Adults diagnosed later can’t join.
qc-pump.howToApply: For supplies, send your original receipts or insurance statements to the program’s paying agent, the CHU de Québec – Université Laval. With some companies you don’t pay for supplies at all, because the CHU refunds the company directly.
qc-pump.notes: The program’s page was last updated on February 19, 2021, so check the current amounts with the program.

nb-ipp.covered: Insulin pumps, pump supplies and glucose sensors (CGM), for the part that isn’t covered by other insurance.
nb-ipp.who: Pumps: type 1, at any age. Sensors: type 1, or type 2 with 3 or more insulin injections a day. It’s based on income, and private insurance has to be used first. If your insurance already covers 100% of the cost, you can’t join.
nb-ipp.howToApply: For pumps, an endocrinologist, internist or pediatrician confirms you meet the medical criteria; for sensors, the health care provider who manages your diabetes does. If you apply for both, the same specialist confirms both. Then you apply online. Devices and supplies come only from the program’s approved vendors, not from pharmacies. You pay your share to the vendor, and the vendor bills the province for the rest.
nb-ipp.notes: Insulin, test strips and batteries aren’t covered by this program.

ns-ipp.covered: One insulin pump every 5 years (Tandem, Medtronic or Insulet), plus pump supplies. You pay a yearly share based on your income and family size, with no premiums or deductibles.
ns-ipp.who: People with type 1 diabetes, diagnosed at least 4 months ago.
ns-ipp.howToApply: Contact the Insulin Pump Program to confirm you’re eligible. It connects you with an approved Diabetes Health Centre, which completes and sends a Clinical Eligibility Form for you. Then fill in the funding application (one form for adults, one for children and youth) and mail it with your supporting documents. A decision takes about 1 to 2 weeks. Renew between January 1 and March 31 every year.
ns-ipp.notes: Glucose sensors aren’t part of this program. Nova Scotia has a separate Sensor-based Glucose Monitoring Program, shown under sensor programs.

pe-ipp.covered: Up to 100% of the cost of a pump and its supplies, shipped every 3 months, depending on your household income, any private insurance and the device’s cost. Approved pumps: Medtronic, Omnipod and Tandem. Glucose sensors aren’t part of it: PEI has a separate Glucose Sensor Program.
pe-ipp.who: PEI residents of any age with type 1 diabetes whom the Provincial Diabetes Program finds medically eligible.
pe-ipp.howToApply: Your family doctor or nurse practitioner can refer you to the Provincial Diabetes Program, whose team decides whether you’re medically eligible. You then complete the program’s application with your pump team. You pay your share straight to the pump company, usually every 3 months before your supplies ship. Renew every year between April 1 and June 30.
pe-ipp.notes: If you have private insurance, its share is taken off before the program works out its own, so ask your insurer for written confirmation of your coverage. What you pay for the pump or its supplies doesn’t count toward the Catastrophic Drug Program’s household cap.

nl-pump.covered: Basic insulin pumps and supplies, for people with type 1 diabetes who qualify. Since January 18, 2021, new clients 18 and over have an income test to work out whether they pay part of the cost, with a financial hardship policy.
nl-pump.who: People with type 1 diabetes who qualify medically. Children and youth up to 18 have full coverage.
nl-pump.notes: These details come from a 2021 government news release. Eastern Health ran the program then, and its pages have since moved, so check the current details with your diabetes team.

yt-pump.covered: Yukon’s National Pharmacare Program gives access to newer insulin pump technology, such as the Omnipod 5 system. Pump eligibility is granted every 5 years.
yt-pump.notes: The program’s page doesn’t say how much of a pump is covered or how to apply. For questions about diabetes equipment or supplies, it points you to Chronic Disease and Disability Benefits or the Senior Pharmacare Program.

on-adp-cgm.covered: Full coverage of real-time CGM sensors and transmitters, and in some cases a receiver, up to a set quantity every 2 years.
on-adp-cgm.who: People with type 1 diabetes who meet the program’s criteria.
on-adp-cgm.howToApply: Your diabetes education program can tell you whether you meet the criteria. Coverage is renewed every 2 years.

on-odb-cgm.covered: Dexcom G7 since July 31, 2025, up to 45 sensors a year, and FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus since November 28, 2025, up to 31 sensors a year, with a receiver or reader.
on-odb-cgm.who: People covered by the Ontario Drug Benefit who take insulin for diabetes. That includes people 65 and over, and people 24 and under with no private plan (OHIP+).
on-odb-cgm.howToApply: You need a prescription from a doctor or nurse practitioner. The pharmacy claims it from the Ontario Drug Benefit.

bc-cgm.covered: Dexcom G6 and G7, FreeStyle Libre 2 and FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus are on PharmaCare’s list of diabetes devices. All of them need Special Authority before PharmaCare will cover them.
bc-cgm.howToApply: Ask your diabetes team or pharmacist about Special Authority before you order.

ab-cgm.covered: Dexcom G6 and G7, FreeStyle Libre 2 and 3 Plus, and Medtronic sensors, up to yearly limits, such as 37 Dexcom G7 sensors or 25 FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus sensors. Co-payments apply, and sensors don’t count toward the yearly limit on diabetes supplies.
ab-cgm.who: Albertans enrolled in one of Alberta’s government-sponsored health benefit plans. Under 18: any ongoing insulin or insulin pump therapy. 18 and over: an insulin pump, a basal-bolus insulin or a premixed insulin.
ab-cgm.howToApply: Get your sensors at a pharmacy. For adults, Medtronic sensors need Special Authorization first.
ab-cgm.notes: Since October 1, 2026, these plans pay only after any private or workplace plan you have.

mb-cgm.covered: Continuous and flash glucose monitors, through regular Pharmacare. Your Pharmacare deductible applies.
mb-cgm.who: Type 1 or type 2 diabetes managed with several insulin injections a day (basal-bolus) or an insulin pump.
mb-cgm.howToApply: You don’t need a special application.

qc-cgm.covered: FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus (listed since December 11, 2025) and Dexcom G6 and G7 are on Quebec’s public plan list as exception drugs. Since February 4, 2026, the same criteria apply to every continuous glucose monitor on the list.
qc-cgm.who: People 2 and over. Under 18: type 1 diabetes. 18 and over: intensive insulin therapy (an insulin pump, or at least 3 injections a day of at least 2 different insulins), plus at least one of these: an A1C that stays above your target despite optimal care, frequent lows in the past year, or not being able to recognize or report the signs of a low.
qc-cgm.howToApply: Your prescriber asks for coverage as an exception. The first approval lasts 6 months. It’s renewed if you wear the sensor at least 70% of the time.
qc-cgm.notes: Quebec’s public plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec. Check the details with RAMQ.

ns-sbgm.covered: Approved sensors and supplies listed in the Nova Scotia Formulary, dispensed by a pharmacy with a prescription. There’s a yearly deductible based on family income: $0 up to $60,000, $500 up to $80,000, $750 up to $100,000 and $1,000 up to $150,000. There are no premiums or co-payments.
ns-sbgm.who: Nova Scotia residents aged 2 and over with a valid Health Card and a household income of $150,000 or less, with type 1 or type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin therapy (at least 4 injections a day) or an insulin pump.
ns-sbgm.howToApply: Fill in the registration form (a doctor, nurse practitioner or pharmacist completes its last page) and submit it online or by mail. Enrolment takes 1 to 2 weeks and renews automatically each February. You pay the full cost at the pharmacy until you reach your deductible.
ns-sbgm.notes: Private insurance has to be used first. The program doesn’t cover prescriptions bought outside Nova Scotia except in very specific cases.

nl-cgm.covered: Full or partial coverage of glucose sensors (CGM).
nl-cgm.who: In May 2025, the province announced that from fall 2025 the program would be open to everyone with type 1 diabetes who meets its medical and income criteria.
nl-cgm.notes: The program started in 2023 for children with type 1. In 2024 it grew to include young people up to age 24, and pregnancy and gestational diabetes. Ask the program what it covers for you now.

on-odb-strips.covered: Test strips each year: 3,000 if you use insulin; 400 if you take a diabetes medicine with a higher risk of lows; 200 with a lower-risk medicine; 200 if you manage with diet and lifestyle alone. More needs a reason from your doctor or nurse practitioner.
on-odb-strips.who: People covered by the Ontario Drug Benefit. That includes people 65 and over, and people 24 and under with no private plan (OHIP+).

on-mfhp.covered: 75% of the cost of a blood glucose meter, up to $75 once every 5 years, and 75% of the cost of test strips and lancets, up to $920 a year. For a talking meter, if a letter from your doctor confirms visual impairment, up to $300 once every 5 years.
on-mfhp.who: People who use insulin (type 1 or type 2), and people with gestational diabetes, who have no other coverage for these supplies. If you’re 65 or over, on social assistance or a Trillium Drug Program client, you can claim only for lancets and a blood glucose meter.
on-mfhp.howToApply: Diabetes Canada runs this program for Ontario. Your first claim form has to be signed by a doctor or nurse practitioner. Mail in the claim form with your original receipts. Processing takes about 8 weeks.

on-adp-seniors.covered: $170 a year toward insulin syringes and needles.
on-adp-seniors.who: People 65 and over who need insulin every day and live at home.
on-adp-seniors.howToApply: Buy them from any retailer in Ontario that sells them. Renew every 2 years. ADP pays you by direct deposit or cheque.

bc-np-supplies.covered: Since April 1, 2026, up to 400 lancets, 300 alcohol swabs and 100 blood or urine ketone strips a year, through Fair PharmaCare and Plans C, F and W (100% on Plans C, F and W). Coverage is processed at the pharmacy counter.
bc-np-supplies.who: You need training from a diabetes education centre or primary care network first. If you’re not on Plan C, F or W, register for Fair PharmaCare.

nl-strips.covered: Test strips a year: 2,500 with short-acting insulin; 700 with long-acting insulin only, plus 100 more with Special Authorization; 100 with non-insulin diabetes medicines only, plus 50; 50 with no diabetes medicine, plus 50 (fills 6 months apart). In pregnancy with gestational or type 2 diabetes, the quantity your health professional asks for.
nl-strips.who: People covered by the Newfoundland and Labrador Prescription Drug Program. A strip claim is paid only if a claim for a diabetes medicine was paid for you in the past year, or you have Special Authorization.
nl-strips.notes: The program pays last: if you have private insurance, the claim goes there first.

yt-cddb.covered: Diabetes is one of the program’s listed conditions. It can help with supplies such as syringes and glucose test kits, and equipment such as glucometers, when your health practitioner recommends them.
yt-cddb.howToApply: Your doctor applies to the program for you, before you buy. If you buy outside Yukon, you need the program’s approval first, or you pay and claim it back within 1 year.
yt-cddb.notes: It pays last: claim from any workplace or private plan first. There’s a yearly deductible.

nt-ehb.covered: Extended Health Benefits cover prescribed medical supplies and equipment on the NIHB Medical Supplies and Equipment list. Above income band 10, EHB pays 75% until your family reaches its maximum of $500 to $1,500. Income bands 2 to 10 pay nothing for now, and seniors 60 and over pay nothing.
nt-ehb.notes: We haven’t confirmed on an official page how EHB covers diabetes devices, so ask the program. EHB pays last. First Nations and Inuit residents use NIHB, and Métis residents the Métis Health Benefits Program.

mb-mepp.covered: Since April 15, 2025, most diabetes medicines at no cost and with no deductible. Ozempic isn’t included.
mb-mepp.howToApply: Bring your prescription and your Manitoba Health card to any Manitoba pharmacy.
mb-mepp.notes: Pumps, glucose sensors, test strips, syringes and lancets aren’t part of it. Glucose sensors and supplies are covered under regular Pharmacare, where your deductible applies. Adult insulin pumps are covered at no cost by a separate program, shown under pump programs.

bc-plan-np.covered: Since March 1, 2026, insulin and a set list of other diabetes medicines at no cost. A few others need Special Authority. Wider coverage of devices and supplies began on April 1, 2026.
bc-plan-np.who: It’s automatic if you’re enrolled in MSP. The prescription must be dispensed in B.C.

pe-pharmacare.covered: Since May 1, 2025, many diabetes medicines at no cost at any community pharmacy in PEI. Test strips cost $11 per 100 if you’re enrolled in PEI Pharmacare’s Diabetes Drug Program; with insulin, 100 strips up to every 25 days. Insulin syringes and pen needles aren’t covered.
pe-pharmacare.who: PEI residents with a valid PEI Health Card. Members of a federal plan, such as NIHB or Veterans Affairs Canada, keep that plan.
pe-pharmacare.notes: Prescriptions filled at a pharmacy outside PEI aren’t covered.

yt-pharmacare.covered: Diabetes medicines listed in the Yukon Drug Formulary are free at Yukon pharmacies, and the program pays first, even if you have private insurance. If you choose a brand-name drug when a lower-cost one is available, you pay the difference. It doesn’t cover diabetes equipment, supplies or glucose monitors, or medicines such as Ozempic.
yt-pharmacare.who: Yukon residents with Yukon health care coverage who aren’t covered by a federal drug program, such as NIHB or Veterans Affairs Canada. Enrolment is automatic.
yt-pharmacare.notes: Medicines filled outside Yukon aren’t covered.

fed-pharmacare.covered: The Pharmacare Act became law on October 10, 2024. Each province and territory has to sign its own agreement before anything changes where you live.
fed-pharmacare.notes: The federal government also announced a Diabetes Device Fund for devices and supplies in February 2024. The announcement said its details would follow discussions with the provinces and territories. We haven’t found an official page that says how to use it.

fed-dtc.covered: A tax credit for people whose impairment meets the CRA’s test. For diabetes, the usual route is life-sustaining therapy.
fed-dtc.who: If you have type 1, the CRA treats you as meeting the life-sustaining therapy test, from 2021 on. Otherwise, the therapy has to be needed at least 2 times a week, for an average of at least 14 hours a week, and the need has to have lasted, or be expected to last, at least 12 months. Time your pump spends delivering insulin doesn’t count toward the 14 hours.
fed-dtc.howToApply: Apply online or by phone with the CRA’s digital form, or by mail with the paper form T2201. Both parts of the application have to go in the same way. Even with type 1, you still have to apply.

fed-rdsp.covered: A long-term savings plan, with government grants and bonds.
fed-rdsp.who: You have to be approved for the Disability Tax Credit first, live in Canada and have a Social Insurance Number. You can open a plan until December 31 of the year you turn 59. Grants and bonds are paid only until the year you turn 49.

fed-medical-expenses.covered: What no program pays for may be claimable as a medical expense on your tax return. The CRA’s list includes insulin, needles and syringes, insulin pens, an insulin pump with its disposable parts, and a device to measure blood sugar, each with a prescription.

privateFirst.AB: Since October 1, 2026, Alberta’s government-sponsored programs, the Insulin Pump Therapy Program included, pay only after any private or workplace plan, so your private plan pays first. Tell your pharmacist about all the coverage you have.
privateFirst.NB: New Brunswick’s Insulin Pump Program covers only the part other insurance doesn’t, so your private plan pays first.
privateFirst.NS: Nova Scotia’s Insulin Pump Program pays after any other coverage you have, so your private plan pays first.
privateFirst.PE: PEI’s Insulin Pump Program takes off what your private insurance covers before it works out its own share, so your private plan pays first. Ask your insurer for written confirmation of your coverage.

liivv.pharmacies: Liivv’s pharmacies serve all of Canada, Quebec and the territories included. Insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec.
liivv.askUsTitle: Can we bill your program for you?
liivv.askUsBody: Our pharmacy in your province bills your provincial drug plan directly for what it covers, except in Quebec. For other programs, it depends on how each one pays: where one pays you back, ask us for an invoice for your claim. Ask us before you order and we’ll tell you where things stand.
liivv.quebecBody: Liivv’s pharmacies serve Quebec, but insulin can’t be ordered online for delivery in Quebec. Quebec’s public drug plan generally doesn’t cover prescription drugs bought outside Quebec, so orders shipped to Quebec are paid for privately. For pump supplies, the Insulin Pump Access Program takes receipts, as shown below: ask us for an invoice for your claim.
liivv.territoryBody: Liivv’s pharmacies serve the territories too. Our pharmacies are in the provinces, so you pay for your order yourself. Check with your program that it will take your receipt before you order, and ask us for an invoice for your claim.

governance.disclaimer: This is general information, not medical or financial advice. It isn’t a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist, and it doesn’t tell you which device or medicine to use. Programs change their amounts and rules often, so check the official page or ask the program before you plan around a number.

type-1.title: Type 1
type-1.heroBody: Insulin every day, lows and ketones, sensors and pumps: the cards that matter most with type 1, in one order.

body.1: With type 1, your pancreas makes no insulin, so you take insulin by injection or with a pump. Diabetes Canada says 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1, and it can start in adulthood too. Breakthrough T1D estimates that about 71% of people with type 1 in Canada were diagnosed as adults.
body.2: This path puts the cards that matter most with type 1 in one order. They cover how to treat a low and when to check for ketones, the sensors, pens and pumps you may use, and the times in life when the details change. Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline prefers automated insulin delivery for anyone willing and able to use it, so the pump and sensor cards are here too. Your team decides your plan with you.

type-2.title: Type 2
type-2.heroBody: From the first numbers to the yearly checkups: the cards that matter most with type 2, in one order.

body.1: Type 2 is the most common type. Diabetes Canada says 90 to 95% of people with diabetes in Canada have it, and it may cause no symptoms at all. Treatment is different for each person. Diabetes Canada says many people with type 2 need insulin to stay healthy. Whether you do, and when, is decided with your team.
body.2: This path starts with the basics. Next come checking your blood sugar at home and the times a low can happen, then the checkups that look after your feet, eyes, kidneys and heart. If your diabetes doesn’t fit the usual picture, read Could my type be different? Breakthrough T1D says LADA, a type 1 that starts slowly in adults, is often first treated as type 2.

gestational.title: Gestational diabetes
gestational.heroBody: During your pregnancy, and the test that comes after the birth: the cards that matter most with gestational diabetes, in one order.

body.1: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found during pregnancy. Diabetes Canada says it affects 3 to 20% of pregnancies and usually goes away after the birth. Screening for it is offered between 24 and 28 weeks, or earlier if you’re at higher risk. Many people manage it with healthy eating and activity. Some also need medicine, such as insulin.
body.2: It still matters after the birth. Diabetes Canada says it raises the chance of type 2 later, for you and your child, and recommends a glucose tolerance test between 6 weeks and 6 months after the birth. This path covers your pregnancy first, then the reminder for afterwards. If you had diabetes before you were pregnant, read Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 instead.

prediabetes.title: Prediabetes
prediabetes.heroBody: What your numbers mean, and the everyday cards on food and movement.

body.1: Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal, but not high enough to be called type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Canada says not everyone with prediabetes goes on to develop type 2, but many people do.
body.2: This path keeps to the everyday: what your numbers mean, and the cards on food and movement. If losing weight is right for you, Diabetes Canada says healthy changes that lead to a loss of 5% of your starting weight can delay or prevent type 2. Regular activity also lowers your risk, and a registered dietitian can help you find changes that suit you. Ask your doctor what your numbers mean for you, and when to test again.

intro.heading: When your type is less common

body.1: Most people have type 1 or type 2, but Diabetes Canada says some cases are difficult to classify. Its guideline lists other forms too. These include LADA, a type 1 that starts slowly in adults, and single-gene types such as MODY. Diabetes can also be linked to the pancreas, cystic fibrosis, iron overload or some medicines, and it can start after a transplant.
body.2: The right type matters, because Diabetes Canada says it may change your treatment. This path starts with the clues worth raising with your team, then gives each less common type its own card. Cards that rest on international guidance say so. Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything here. Any change is made with your specialist.
